speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ORDERS FOR CUSTODY AND COROLLARY RELIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill sets forth two amendments to the Divorce Act. The first amendment is so technical that I shall not trespass upon the time of the House. It cannot be explained briefly but the explanatory note with the bill puts the argument totally and fairly.
The second amendment would allow courts in provinces to which a successful party has moved to examine orders. If a person has obtained in Newfoundland an order for corollary relief and has moved to British Columbia, instead of putting those concerned to the expense of going back to the court in
Newfoundland the order could be reviewed in the courts of British Columbia.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, December 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill S-8, to amend the Trust Companies Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION. OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, four such bills have been taken off the list of private members' bills and have been transferred to government orders with the result that these companies will be brought under the jurisdiction of the Superintendent of Insurance. This raises a number of points which should be seriously considered by hon. members of the House. Most hon. members did not seriously consider the implications of many bills passed during private members' hour, but I believe there is a

considerable role to be played by our financial institutions other than banks or nearbanks. I believe the trust companies, small loan companies and insurance companies fall into that category because a large amount of money is held in trust by these various agencies which operate for the Canadian public.
A great deal of this money is never returned to the people whom we feel should obtain the benefits of it. These are mainly the people who have to issue debentures for municipal, provincial or large social capital expenditures. This money in the main has not been available. For this reason we believe the proliferation of trust companies, insurance companies and small loan companies really cuts into the role which I think all Canadians believe should be played by the banking institutions. The role of these companies has not been supervised to the degree certain other financial institutions have been. These companies have had difficulty in getting their bills passed and the government has taken the easy way out and has now provided for their incorporation by letters patent. Therefore the Superintendent of Insurance will have a great deal more responsibility than he had before.
These trust companies have operated under a certain set of regulations. They have been supervised in the past, but when we establish such new companies by letters patent I believe we should give some consideration to the operations of the existing companies and consider whether or not new companies are needed. Nowhere in this bill do I see any power given to the Superintendent of Insurance that would allow him to make such a decision. It is a fact that a small, private trust company is set up it will come back to the Superintendent of Insurance in a year or two asking for an increase in its capitalization. In two or three years it might even be able to afford a $5 million capitalization.
These trust companies have grown at an alarming rate over the years. So whether or not we should incorporate other trust companies becomes very important, considering the role they play in the financial structure of Canada, the role they play in relation to lending institutions and the role they should play in respect of lending money for long-term social capital purposes such as the building of private homes, hospitals and schools. This role has been limited so far as the trust companies are concerned. It is obviously limited as far as the interest return rate is concerned. But there are many fields in which the trust
January 23, 1970

companies have jurisdiction over administration, such as with respect to estates, bankruptcies and business operations run by a third party, where they would be able to invest the large sums of money they have in stable investments.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I am very pleased to note that under the terms of the new legislation we will allow the trust companies to invest in such things as the Industrial Development Bank. We are allowing them to make loans under the terms of the small loans legislation. We are allowing them to make loans to farmers under farm credit legislation. In general we are allowing them to make loans in those fields in which the government assumes some responsibility for the repayment of loans. In this way we are broadening the role of the trust companies.
I am sure there are many Members of Parliament who do not really care one way or another what a particular trust company does. Many of us are not too interested either in what a particular insurance company does. But, Mr. Speaker, we should be concerned about what these companies do in the aggregate. As Members of Parliament we have not been pleased about some things that have happened in individual trust companies and insurance companies. For instance, in my experience Allstate is about as close to being crooked as it could be. People who submit claims to Allstate sometimes find they have to wait four or five years to have their claims settled. This is not generally true of insurance companies. While I am interested in this particular insurance company for that reason, I am more interested in the broad spectrum of insurance companies. The same is true with respect to a trust company which may have mismanaged a bankruptcy. It attracts our attention.
Insurance companies, trust companies and loan companies are playing an increasing role in our society. They affect many people who are not at all involved with estates, the administration of estates, bankruptcies, and the administration of bankruptcies. The difficulty the individual has is in arriving at a reasonable personal role in his relationship with these institutions.
I have mentioned one particular insurance company. I do not think the House should be concerned with the actual methods that insurance companies use, but when a complaint about one company comes to the attention of
Trust Companies Act
a Member of Parliament he must wonder if this situation applies to all insurance companies and whether it is not the tip of an iceberg, the tip of one huge problem about which something should be done. I would like to see Members of Parliament become much more interested in the over-all operations of trust companies and in the role they play in the daily life of our communities.
It seems to me that the House is being asked to pass these four bills in order to end a problem that I helped to create. I make no apology for that, Mr. Speaker, even though on a number of occasions we used incorporation bills, and in some cases may have abused them, for a definite purpose. I think our purpose has been accomplished. However, I would not like to see this bill pass without saying that we had no intention of chasing all the financial institutions into the department of the Superintendent of Insurance.
Over the past ten years we have had close relations with the Superintendent of Insurance. I have known very well both of the gentlemen who in recent years have occupied that position and have found them to be very capable people. However, I am well aware of their limitations with respect to staff and organization which may prevent that department from carrying on the type of supervision that, hopefully, people thought would be done when incorporation bills were being examined by Parliament. I know that most members of the House never looked at incorporation bills. In fact the Senate did a heck of a lot more work than the House in supervising incorporations, even though in many cases it did so for the wrong reason, because Senators were to be on the boards of directors of the companies seeking incorporation. Anyway, at least the Senate took a look at incorporation bills, but most members of the House did not stay in the chamber when such bills were being discussed.
I am scared that we are giving the Superintendent of Insurance a responsibility which I think he cannot exercise, a responsibility which I think he does not want, and a responsibility which I do not think we should make him exercise. He will now have to look at these bills in the light of the public good. That is a loose form of wording. We used to have it in most union constitutions. At the end of our meetings when there was nothing else to discuss we wound up discussing the good of the union, found out who were the sick people in hospital, sent them flowers and arranged for somebody to visit them. Maybe

January 23, 1970
Trust Companies Act
we should do that now in terms oi some of the financial institutions that will be incorporated through letters patent.
We may quite easily find that another 100 or 200 trust companies will be incorporated. If this happens we will find 100 new offices on Sparks Street. Such companies always seem to have a great deal of money for elaborate offices. You see them giving away little cars or silverware in order to attract new depositors who agree to leave their money on deposit over a long period of time. Each time this happens it means that that much money is not available in the form of normal savings subject to the control of the Bank of Canada.
That money will be spread out over many companies, as is the case now with insurance companies, so that in the end it will be difficult to consider it as savings of the public. It will not be a viable resource which one can spend or borrow against, as can be done in the banks. I wonder who will look after that. In its wisdom both Houses of Parliament used to scrutinize proposed incorporations bills on their merits. Now we are turning them over to the Superintendent of Insurance and giving up our responsibility, and I do not see that this bill provides any protection through powers given to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) or to other ministers who are concerned with financial institutions.
[DOT] (12 noon)
If we say to the Superintendent of Insurance, "It is now your job, you have to supervise this," I think he will be hard pressed to do so, and I think he will be very unhappy trying to do it, although I am sure he will do the best job he can. I think the government should be prepared to write in some protection for the public and provide guidelines for the Superintendent of Insurance by which he can make the decisions that we will now be asking him to make. I have read the bill and I know there are a number of worth-while changes in it. However, I think the philosophic problems of our financial institutions should not become a pawn in my objections to some of the bills submitted in Private Members' hour. I suggest that the minister may find us very sympathetic if he is willing to provide the type of protection that we had hoped for, and were working towards in the Private Members' hour, for trust companies and the public from abuses apparent in the past and that in the future will be multiplied tenfold.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION. OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the previous speaker, the hon.

member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) was speaking primarily to item No. 44 on the order paper, resuming debate on Bill S-8. My comments, which will be very brief will be dealing with items 42, 43, 44 and 45, the four financial bills concerning insurance companies, trust companies and loan companies.
In making a general statement which will be applicable to all four items, I might say that these bills are significant and important pieces of legislation. The role of the insurance companies, trust companies and loan companies in the financial and commercial life of Canada is such as to affect every Canadian in his lifetime and is a most important part of the private sector of the Canadian economy. In another sense, however, they are housekeeping bills. The changes that have occurred in the corporate structure, in the organization and in the function of the various kinds of financial houses in recent years, require that we review, revise and up-date our legislation on such companies in the light of these changes and in the light of the relationships between these companies and the citizens.
Basically, therefore, the only principle at issue here is the need for modernization of the laws defining these corporations. The same principle that was applicable to our loan companies and chartered banks is applicable to our general laws on corporations.
All these bills can best be considered in committee where the highly technical changes can be examined with the help of public service officials and private citizens. Generally, these changes can be said to broaden the power of these companies and also the power of government to control the affairs of the companies. It is in this area that we intend to scrutinize these bills thoroughly in committee to ensure that in granting such powers to private industry and government, and in balancing these powers one against the other, the over-all balance is struck in the public interest.
I have one other observation to make, Mr. Speaker, which is irrelevant in the immediate sense I admit, but very relevant to the business of the House. All these bills went through the other place in the last session and at least two of them then appeared on the Order Paper in this House. All of them died before being passed at the close of the last session and this session they had to be reintroduced. It seems to me that some thought might be given to changing our rules to provide that within the life of a Parliament a bill
January 23, 1970

might go over from one session to another, maintaining the place on the order paper in the new session that it had on the prorogation of the previous session.
That is all I have to say at this moment, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
that Bill S-9, to amend the Loan Companies Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make clear that I did not make use of my right of reply at the end of debate on second reading of the previous matter, and with the accord of the members of the House with respect to the second reading of this bill and the two that follow, I propose to forgo my forthcoming right of reply in order to expedite the business of the House. However, I wish it to be understood that it is my intention to deal with points raised by hon. members when these bills are before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for study. At this time, I wish to put on record an outline of the amendments to the Loan Companies Act intended by the bill now before us.
The Loan Companies Act is an act that applies to companies that might be more accurately described as mortgage loan companies. Their essential characteristic is the making of mortgage loans on real estate or the investment in such mortgage loans. The funds for this purpose are raised by the sale of debentures to the public or by the acceptance of deposits. At the present time, there are 12 such companies active in Canada having total assets of about $1.5 billion and liabilities to the public of about $1.3 billion. The extent of their involvement in real estate mortgages is illustrated by the fact that more than 80 per cent of their assets are of this type.
The principal amendments contemplated by this bill fall into four categories. Firstly, the amendments would effect certain changes in
Loan Companies Act
the investment powers of loan companies generally in the direction of expanding such powers and bringing them closely into line with powers of life insurance companies. One of the most significance perhaps would be an amendment to enable companies to make investments and loans within their own discretion up to a maximum limit of 7 per cent of the total assets of the company. This corresponds to the so-called basket provision that has been in effect for life insurance companies for some years. There has been a basket provision provided in the legislation for mortgage loan companies but this was limited to 15 per cent of the company's capital and surplus.
Companies would be empowered to invest in real estate for the production of income, not only where the real estate is leased to a company whose stocks are eligible investments, but also real estate that qualifies on an earnings test. Also, the size of individual parcels of real estate that might be purchased would be increased from 1 per cent to 2 per cent of a company's assets. These changes would bring the powers of loan companies into line with those for insurance companies with respect to investments in real estate for the production of income.
The requirement for a minimum statutory margin with respect to collateral loans would be removed and companies could determine their own margin, subject, however, to their having sufficient collateral to cover the amount of the loan on a market value basis.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Companies may now make mortgages subject to the limitation that the amount of the mortgage is not to exceed 75 per cent of the value of the real estate. They may lend in excess of this amount, however, where the excess is guaranteed or insured by a governmental agency. An amendment is proposed that would permit excess mortgages to be made if the excess is insured under a policy of mortgage insurance issued by a registered insurance company.
The power to make investments and loans in corporate securities would be expanded to enable a company to invest in such securities outside Canada in any country in which the company is doing business. A company would be required however to maintain assets in Canada at all times at least equal to its liabilities in Canada. The power of companies to own subsidiaries would be expanded to enable a loan company to operate a loan com-

January 23. 1970
Loan Companies Act
pany subsidiary in a foreign jurisdiction and to incorporate a subsidiary investment company for the purpose of selling mutual fund shares. It would also be able to own subsidiary companies for the purpose of carrying on any business reasonably ancillary to that of a loan company. The power to own subsidiaries would be subject to terms and conditions as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council.
The existing prohibition against loan companies making loans on the security of promissory notes would be repealed, thus enabling companies to make consumer loans within the limitation prescribed by the basket provision should they so desire. There has been some interest in this possibility by some loan companies, particularly those in the business of accepting deposits from customers, many of whom have been asking if this kind of loan could be made to them.
The second principal amendment, somewhat related to investment powers, is one that would expand the existing prohibition against loans to directors or officers to prohibit loans to or investments in any major shareholder. Also, loans to or investments in other corporations would be prohibited if a director, officer or major shareholder had a significant interest in that other corporation. These amendments are for the purpose of expanding the existing prohibitions against investment transactions that may involve a conflict of interest on the part of persons who are in a position to control or direct the investment decisions of the loan company.
The third main category relates to changes in the system of supervision and control, particularly with respects to companies that may find themselves in financial difficulties. At present, the minister has power to insert conditions or limitations in a company's licence when it is renewed, from year to year, and he may also withdraw the licence if the superintendent reports that, in his opinion, the assets of the company are insufficient to enable it to continue in business. There is, however, no intermediate step between inserting conditions in the licence and withdrawing it.
The amendments propose that the superintendent be required to report to the minister in any case where he thinks that a company is getting into financial difficulties or where it has exceeded its borrowing limits. The minister would then be empowered to take one or more of three steps. He could impose conditions in the company's licence; he could prescribe a time within which the company

would be required to remedy the defect or he could direct the superintendent to take control of the company's assets.
In any case where the superintendent has control of the assets of a company, the minister could request the Attorney General to apply to a court to direct the superintendent to take control of the company for the purpose of its rehabilitation or he could request the Attorney General to apply to a court for an order winding up the company under the Winding-up Act.
Where the superintendent has control of a company for rehabilitation or has control of the assets of a company he would be empowered to assess expenses incurred by him in this connection against other loan companies.
The superintendent would be empowered to take control of a company's assets temporarily in any case where he found there had been an improper accounting of the assets. This could be maintained only for a period of seven days at the discretion of the superintendent. Any longer period would require ministerial authorization.
These changes are proposed with a view to providing a more flexible system of supervision and control in cases where companies are in financial difficulties and where action requires to be taken to protect the interests of depositors and debenture holders.
The fourth category of amendments deals with changes in the system of incorporating companies and amending existing charters. At present, mortgage loan companies may be incorporated federally only by special act of Parliament. Amendments to existing charters may also be made only by special act. The proposed amendments would adopt a letters patent system for incorporating new companies and for amending existing charters. It is also proposed to enable provincial companies to change to the status of federally incorporated companies by a letters patent procedure subject to concurrence of the home province. As in the case of the proposed amendments to the Insurance Companies Act and the Trust Companies Act, the letters patent would be issued by the Corporations Branch of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, subject however to the concurrence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). Investigation would be made by the Superintendent of Insurance in the manner now followed in respect of private bills and public notice would be required in the Canada Gazette for application for incorporation.
January 23, 1970

The letters patent would be in standard form as provided in the bill, but enough flexibility would be permitted to enable the letters patent to be adjusted to meet special circumstances. In particular, if the persons proposing the incorporation so desired, letters patent could contain restrictions on voting rights or on share ownership. Similar restrictions could be put in the charters of existing companies if the application were approved at a special general meeting of the company and if the Minister of Finance concurs.
The amendments would provide that before a new company can be authorized to transact business it must have a minimum capital of at least $500,000. At present, the minimum initial capital is set in each private bill and thus considered on a case-by-case basis by Parliament.
Apart from the four main categories just described, there are a number of other amendments of significance. I shall touch upon the principal points.
A proposed amendment would require notice to the superintendent in case of a major transfer of shares. This proposes that no transfer of a block of stock in excess of 10 per cent would be permitted until after 30 days' notice to the superintendent including information as to beneficial ownership. Such notice would also be required in cases of transfer of lesser blocks where the result was change of control. This would not grant a veto power to the superintendent or the government but would ensure that supervisory authorities have adequate notice of significant changes in share ownership.
The Governor in Council would be authorized to adopt regulations dealing with the safekeeping of securities and the bonding of directors, officers and employees. It would be intended under this provision to establish procedures designed to improve the care and custody of assets of companies.
At present, companies are limited in the amount of money they can accept on deposit and borrow on the issuance of debentures to a maximum of 15 times their capital and surplus. The amendments would raise this limit to 20 times subject to approval by the Minister of Finance on specific application by the company.
To use words similar to those I used in opening debate on the amendments to the Trust Companies Act, this amendment would make it possible for these companies to make more money available for mortgage lending. An important part of the lending business, as
Loan Companies Act
I said with respect to the Trust Companies Act, is in the field of lending for housing purposes. As I indicated with respect to the trust companies, the minister responsible for housing has told me that companies of this type have been contacting him and stressing the importance of approval of these amendments if their mortgage lending is not to be curtailed and if they are to be able to respond to the minister's requests that they allocate more funds for lending for housing.
The present liquidity test would be revised to require companies to maintain a reserve of at least 20 per cent of their demand deposits and debentures falling due within 100 days in the form of federal or provincial securities or cash.
Quarterly reports would be required from companies showing their assets and liabilities in order to enable the supervisory authorities to keep a close check on liquidity and semiannual reports would be required showing the changes in investments and loans.
It is proposed to insert an age limit of 75 on eligibility to be elected as a director. This would take effect from January 1, 1972 and is similar to a change made in the Bank Act a few years ago.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
A number of changes are proposed in the auditing requirements, principally for the purpose of specifying the qualification of auditors. This is made the same as in the Bank Act. The act presently contains a provision permitting companies to issue share warrants, that is warrants enabling the holder to convert the warrant into a registered share if he so wishes. These are not the same as share purchase warrants, since the warrant concept here is one that enables the bearer to have the share delivered to him on presentation of this warrant. This is not used by any company at the present time and would create certain difficulties with respect to the control of transfer of shares to non-residents. It is proposed, therefore, that this be deleted from the act.
Certain changes are proposed in the provisions restricting non-resident ownership with a view to clarifying the wording and providing for the preservation of voting rights of non-residents where these rights were acquired while a company was exempt from the restrictions. The requirements for issuance of preferred stock would be somewhat simplified as would the requirements having to do with the adoption of by-laws. At least three-quarters of the directors would be

January 23, 1970
Loan Companies Act
required to be Canadian citizens resident in Canada rather than only 50 per cent as at present. This change would follow a similar change for the Bank Act and one proposed for the Trust Companies Act.
A number of other amendments are proposed for the purpose of modifying wording and correcting a few administrative procedures. A number of changes would be made transferring certain other discretionary authority from the Treasury Board to the minister as a consequence of some of the reorganization changes within government departments.
Part II of the Loan Companies Act refers to the licensing of British loan companies to transact business in Canada. There are in fact no such companies and this part has not been used for a great many years. It is proposed, therefore, to repeal the part.
I will be pleased to attempt to respond to more detailed questions when the bill is before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. It is considered that approval of this bill, like approval of the bill to amend the Trust Companies Act, will assist in widening the supply of funds available for mortgage lending and will widen the ability of federally incorporated loan companies to provide services to the public as well as widening the degree of protection available to depositors and others who lend money to these companies under federal incorporation and supervision. I ask for the support of the House at this second reading stage of the debate on this bill.

speechtext: The law provides that companies can seek deposits from the public only up to a certain proportion of their net assets and the volume of loans they make are linked with the deposits they are able to attract. They are loans by way of mortgage. Obviously, when they are as at present approaching or at the ceiling on borrowing from the public, the power that they have to make loans to the public by way of mortgages is thereby limited. If the authority they have under the act to seek deposits is increased, then to the extent they attract deposits, it will follow that their opportunity to make loans to the public by way of mortgage, which is their principal business, will be increased.

It is proposed the ceiling be increased from the present discretionary limit of some 15 times up to 20 times.
With respect to attracting funds, these institutions are basically competing with other financial institutions which may not be directing or investing their funds toward quite the same mix of investments. I think if they are better able to compete with other institutions and generally better able to attract savings from the public because of the present pattern of lending by these institutions, it would follow that the funds likely would be put into investments by way of mortgage loans following the presently existing pattern.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government has placed a great deal of stress on the need for priorities in carrying on public affairs and in the programs that it presents to Parliament. It has attempted to make a considerable show of its own sense of priorities and to create the
January 23, 1970

image which portrays this sense of priorities. It has also tried to impress upon the public, and other members when they try to get their own way in Parliament, the necessity of making sound rational choices when dealing with public business and public affairs. That is all very fine. Of course, it is like motherhood.
Let us put these particular assertions to the test. Where is the government's sense of priorities in relation to the amending of the Loan Companies Act which is now before us? I point out, Mr. Speaker, that the government has placed this bill ahead of many other far more urgent measures on the Order Paper or which have been announced by the government for introduction at this session. Originally this bill was placed ahead of the Canada water bill for consideration, but that was changed after some opposition interventions in the debate on the four finance company bills. Therefore, the Canada water bill has now passed second reading.
The government has placed this bill ahead of measures to bring about a measure of economic stabilization and in order to ensure that we would not have a considerable unemployment problem this winter. It has placed it ahead of measures to help pensioners, to help veterans and to help distressed groups throughout Canada. I refer to western agriculture, problems of the Maritimes, problems of the cities, unemployment which I already mentioned, and the problems of the Indians and Metis. There are other problems I could also mention.
The government placed this bill ahead of the Canada Development Corporation bill which, of course, is a measure that could be used very effectively, if the government so chose, to deal with some of the problems involved in the large degree of foreign ownership of the Canadian economy. This bill is being placed ahead of the Combines Investigation Act revision which has been announced; the motor vehicle safety bill; the labour code amendments which were supposed to come before us, and other labour legislation. It has been placed ahead of the marketing agencies bill which is important to the agricultural industry as a whole; it has been placed ahead of the revisions to the Canada Grain Act, so badly needed to improve our basic marketing situation, one which has caused a great deal of frustration to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) during the past year. The hon. gentleman seems to be experiencing a 21611-35

This bill has been placed ahead of the co-operatives bill which has been promised by the federal government for years. None of these things has been dealt with during this session so far, but the government has insisted that this bill be dealt with. The loan and trust companies legislation had to go forward. The government felt obliged to satisfy the needs of its friends first; it had to make certain that the financial institutions, who already possess a great deal of power in the economy, obtain even more power and privileges.
There are some curious contradictions in government policy at the moment. On one hand, the government is making a great show of its anti-inflation drive and the need to curb unnecessary spending. It is attempting to set a good example-without any great success, I might say-by following a program of restraint. In the process it is restraining some worth-while and necessary programs. On the other hand, through this legislation, it is increasing the power of loan companies to accumulate funds for further investment; it is giving this extra power to the loan companies whose decisions will be based on considerations of commercial profitability and the corporate well-being of the firms concerned rather than the public good. There is no need to tell members of this House that these two things do not necessarily coincide; it is obvious that the direction of private investment decisions does, in many instances, ignore the public interest in addition to ignoring the government's pleas for restraint. This does not deter the government from proceeding blindly with a bill which will further increase the economic power of these financial institutions. It will certainly have an inflationary effect in present circumstances; it will certainly contribute to the inflationary psychology which government spokesmen have referred to so often as being a major obstacle to be overcome.
These trust and loan companies play an important role in the development of Canada within the framework of our present economy. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics noted recently that in the second quarter of 1969 trust companies increased their investment in

January 23, 1970
Loan Companies Act
mortgages by $125 million to bring their total investments in mortgages at mid-1969 to $2.9 billion. Mortgage companies invested an additional $75 million in mortgages during the same period to bring total mortgage holdings at mid-year to $2.3 billion. It is reported that deposits in credit unions, which are also involved on the total picture of the financial institutions, increased in the second quarter of 1969 by a modest amount. Sales finance companies increased their sales finance paper by $172 million during the quarter bringing total holdings of sales finance paper to $4.7 billion. Mutual funds showed sales of shares to investors amounting to $64 million during the quarter.
As the minister indicated when introducing the bill before us, there are some 12 companies operating under the provisions of this legislation at the present time, and, of course, the Superintendent of Insurance has to report on the activities and financial position of these companies in his annual report. I was interested to learn from the Annual Report of the Superintendent of Insurance for the year 1968 that, as the minister pointed out in his remarks, the total admitted assets at book value of the loan companies in Canada incorporated under federal legislation was slightly more than $1.5 billion in 1968, an increase over 1967 amounting to almost exactly 10 per cent, which is certainly an appreciable one. I was interested to learn also that the two largest corporations which make up the bulk of the total figure are the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation, with total assets of some $629 million, and the Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation, with total assets of some $536 million. There are only two other companies whose assets amount to more than $100 million; the others are relatively small in size, the smallest having assets of only $392,000.
What interested me particularly, looking at the operation of the loan companies, was a table in which an attempt was made to classify mortgage lending on real estate on the basis of provincial distribution. Of a total outstanding at the end of 1968 amounting to some $1,235,000,000, more than $588 million- almost half-was invested in the Province of Ontario. This should be noted in the light of the Prime Minister's criticism of the government of Ontario for failing to take adequate steps to deal with inflation. Perhaps some of that criticism was justified. At the same time, here are these loan companies carrying on their operations in a completely unrestricted

way and, of course, we cannot fail to see that there is an extremely high concentration of their mortgage lending in Ontario, the province in which it has been suggested by the federal government that there is the greatest degree of inflationary pressure.
These companies, as we have seen, are able to carry on their operations completely free from the need to pay any regard to considerations of the public interest when making decisions concerning capital investment and spending across Canada. We know very well that much of Ontario has developed into what might be called the industrial heartland of Canada, and, of course, there is a tendency, when there is no restriction on private investment, for an increasingly large proportion of capital investment, particularly private capital investment, to become concentrated within such an area.
Then again, an extremely complex structure develops in time among these corporations and the financial institutions with which they are related. There are many links between these corporations and companies. Looking at the lists of directors of the two largest corporations to which I referred a few moments ago I find that many of these people are businessmen, well-known Canadian industrialists and financial leaders, who have close interests in many other corporations and areas of economic activity centred in Ontario.

There are regulations, now concerning the investments of loan companies. Loan companies may lend money on certain types of security, such as their assets, up to a total of 20 per cent of the value of securities issued by the company. The borrowing powers of the company are also subject to certain regulations. Up to the present time, the company could obtain money for lending purposes by issuing bonds and debentures and certain other securities or by receiving deposits up to an aggregate of the capital stock of the company and the cash on hand.
I was very interested to take note of some of the remarks of the minister who introduced this bill with respect to the expanded investment powers to be granted to loan companies. Again, it seems to me that the unrestricted expansion of these investment powers comes into direct conflict with some of the other enunciated objectives of the federal government in dealing with our present economic situation. The loan companies are to be given the power to invest in real estate. Their
January 23. 1970

borrowing powers are to be extended, and, in addition, amendments are proposed that would facilitate the amalgamation and purchase of similar companies. This of course can lead to a further concentration of economic power in Canada. We also note that the capacity of the company to borrow or to accept guaranteed trust funds is to be expanded from 15 times the excess of assets over liabilities to 20 times that amount. Again, it seems to me that the unrestricted expansion of these powers comes into direct conflict with the federal government's policies and objectives at the present time.
One other item of which careful note should be taken is the matter of interest rates. This matter of course has been the subject of extensive study by the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee of the House. It is likely that they will be bringing their report before the House in the near future. But it seems to me that this legislation should also be considered in the light of interest rates as they affect the Canadian economy. The fact is that there are many businesses throughout Canada which are finding it difficult to finance with the present rate of interest rates, and those people who are in a weaker economic position find the present situation most trying and difficult. The fact is that large corporations, when they find it necessary to go beyond their own internal sources of funds, when they find that the funds that they can generate internally are now inadequate for their purposes and they have to go to the market in order to borrow money, have a very much easier time in many respects in dealing with their problems and in carrying out the necessary financing than people who do not have a large degree of economic power.
The minister gave an outline of some of the changes that are to be made in the legislation, and one of the items to which he made reference was the change to be made in the incorporation of loan companies. This item has already been commented upon in the debate on the trust companies bill, but I think the point should be emphasized again in dealing with loan companies. I think it is inconceivable that we should have, on the one hand, legislation that gives these companies even more powers than they have at the present time while, on the other hand, we take away from Parliament the power to examine their operations and to examine the proposed corporate structures before giving them the authority to carry on their operations within 21611-351
Loan Companies Act
the Canadian economy. As a matter of fact, before letters patent are granted, if I understand the sections of the bill correctly, there is no requirement to disclose who is involved in establishing a new loan company with the exception of listing the five provisional directors. No doubt other information will be elicited when the company attempts to apply for incorporation, but it seems to me that we need to have a great deal more information, we need to have many more checks and controls, before this power of incorporation is taken away from Parliament.
We also find that there are to be changes with respect to the election of directors. We find now that directors can be elected at the annual meeting rather than by ballot of shareholders. This, of course, will further enable certain people and shareholders with large blocks of shares to obtain even greater power within the scope of these companies' operations. One of the provisions that the government will no doubt try to underline in some discussions is that three quarters of the directors must be Canadian residents and citizens. I think this is certainly a very feeble attempt to deal with the storm of protest that is arising concerning the problem of the foreign ownership of many sectors of the Canadian economy. Certainly, it will not deal with the problem adequately.
If I understand the provisions of the bill correctly, the powers of these companies are to be extended with respect to their ability to make investments in foreign loan companies. It seems to me that this is a point of some concern, because in dealing with the problem of foreign ownership in the Canadian economy one of the problems with which we have had to contend has been the considerable leakage of Canadian capital into other countries and away from Canada. Of course, this increases our need to resort to foreign sources of capital in order to bring about an acceptable level of economic development in Canada. Here we are giving these companies more powers to spend Canadian money and Canadian savings abroad than they possessed previously.
Other restrictions are also being removed. I already noted that the lending ratio is to be increased from 15 to 20 based on the excess of assets over liabilities.
There are a few other technical changes which are also proposed in the bill, but it seems to me that this bill, as it is presented by the government, is totally inadequate-within the framework of the situation facing

January 23, 1970
Loan Companies Act
the economy at present. I suggest that there are five areas of amendments that apply to this bill, and which I think should he considered by the government, before we can consider this legislation to be acceptable and to be anywhere near adequate to deal with our present problems.
The first requirement is that all financial institutions must be brought under the jurisdiction of the Bank of Canada. Second, we also need to give the Bank of Canada authority to alter the lending ratio of companies. Third, we need to ensure that the public interest is considered adequately by having a government appointee on each board of directors of these companies. Fourth, we should ensure that a certain percentage-possibly 15 per cent, which is one figure to which reference has been made-of the lending and investment funds of these companies be under public policy direction. Fifth, the Bank of Canada should have the power to regulate the rate of return and interest rates.
With respect to the rate of return, I was interested to note in the report of the Superintendent of Insurance that while the paid up capital stock of the loan companies at the end of 1968 amounted to slightly under $45 million, their gross profit during the year- that is before income taxes-amounted to $16,856,000, and that the dividends declared for the year amounted to $7,149,000.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
It certainly seems to me that this is a handsome rate of return on the investments shareholders have made in these companies. It seems to me that we need to consider this legislation within the over-all framework of the needs and the problems faced by the Canadian economy at the present time. I have already taken note of the curious set of priorities exhibited by the Liberal government in introducing this piece of legislation ahead of many other items. It seems to me there are certainly some very serious contradictions involved. This represents a great change from the image the Liberal government tried to portray at one time.
Just recently a correspondent in my constituency sent me an advertisement that had been placed in the Country Guide in June of 1944. This advertisement was placed in the Country Guide by the government of Canada. It is entitled in very large letters, "I Had a Nightmare". The text of it reads:
I dreamed that I paid $5.00 for a haircut and $50.00 for a pair of cardboard shoes. I dreamed that we had no wartime controls on prices, profits or

wages, and that we hadn't had the sense to organize the distribution of supplies ail the way down, the line-[DOT]
I dreamed that because everyone was making more money and spending it, prices were skyrocketing.
-all the stores looked like "fire" sales-with people scrambling to buy before prices went still higher-[DOT]
-panicky people were buying things they didn't need, and hoarding everything they could get their hands on-
I dreamed that everybody had to fight to get more money-and that in this mad race, wages and salaries were falling behind.
I dreamed the hand of everyone was against his neighbour, with each of us blaming the other fellow for his troubles.
-with everybody for himself-no matter what it cost in the long run-and no matter how it hurt the war effort.
Of course, each one of these statements was accompanied by a very suitable and appropriate cartoon. Then, in large letters again', his advertisement read, "Then-thank goodness-I woke up!" The text went on:
-to realize with relief that I live in a country where things are sane and stable-where the cost of living has been kept within bounds.
-to realize that prices and wages-production costs and selling prices-are inseparably linked together.
-to realize that without the safeguards that have headed off inflation, my nightmare might have become a reality!
-to remind myself that the danger is still pressing and that we must continue to hold firm-and that means everybody must play fair and do his part by not trying to get some temporary, fancied advantage at the expense of his fellow Canadians.
That is the conclusion of the text. Then, at the bottom we find this:
This advertisement is one of a series being issued by the Government of Canada to emphasize the importance of preventing further increases in the cost of living now and deflation later.
The Liberal government has come a long way since that time. I do not think, in many respects, that this has been to the advantage of people in Canada, but that is the type of image the government tried to portray at that time. I am sure some of the ministers opposite must blush now when remembering this type of ad that their own government inserted in newspapers and publications across Canada.
I could go on to discuss some of the very serious problems that face Canada in respect of foreign ownership. Just recently Professor Abraham Rotstein of the University of Toronto, Department of Political Economy, appeared before a committee of this House.
January 23, 1970

Let me quote from the Globe and Mail of January 21, 1970 as follows:
Prof. Rotstein noted in testimony before the Commons Committee on External Affairs and National Defence that by 1968, U.S.-based, multi-national corporations had amassed $40-billion in long-term investment in the Canadian economy-80 per cent of the over-all foreign investment.
He went on to state:
"The volume of U.S. investment is growing at a rapid rate and we can no longer allow the issue to be decided by default on our side."
He goes on to give an even fuller outline of some of the problems faced by Canada in dealing with the problem of foreign ownership and the fact that such a large proportion of Canada's industry, Canada's economy and Canadian resources are owned and controlled not by Canadian people, either publicly or privately, but by foreign interests.
Of course, there is no necessary criticism of foreigners, whether they be from the United States or some other country, for having come into Canada to invest their money, if we allow them to do so and place no restrictions or conditions on their entry to this country or on the manner in which they carry on their operations. We are the ones who are at fault. We are the ones who made the mistake. And we are the ones now who are going to have to correct some of the errors of the past.
It is quite evident in the legislation before us that the government is not prepared to take even the first small step necessary to regain control of our economy. It has been stated by many people from time to time that in the long run Canada will only be an outpost of the United States economic empire if this trend continues. This is a matter that should give us serious cause for concern within the structure and framework of the operations of the United States industrial empire. We will be somewhat comparable to some sections of the United States mid-west or far west. We will be in a situation comparable to some of the New England States where in fact they are falling behind the over-all rate of U.S. economic development.
Of course, if we allow this trend to continue, we will simply be one of the smaller hinterlands; one of the small outposts bound within the framework of this vast industrial structure. Thus, we do have to give serious consideration to this problem. We do have to reverse the trend. I suggest the only way to reverse this trend is through public action and through government action and intervention. The fact is that today it is necessary to take stronger action to deal with this problem and
Loan Companies Act
to bring it under control than would have been necessary during the past decade.
I have a few more comments I should like to make on this particular matter. Therefore, I should like to call it one o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, prior to the
adjournment at one o'clock I had spent some time discussing some of the provisions in the bill. I am in accord with the remarks of the minister when he stated that some of the details could be discussed at the committee stage. Of course, there are a number of housekeeping provisions in the bill which can be considered quite adequately at that time. Basically, these are provisions in respect of which we have no objection. Our basic objection to this bill is in respect of the context and framework within which it was introduced. This is the reason I want to place before Parliament our point of view. I am the only member of the New Democratic Party who will take part in this debate on this bill at this time. I believe it is necessary that we place our stand on the record. However, I have no wish to prolong the debate. I understand there is a desire in some quarters of the House to proceed with the debate on the proposed Salt Water Fish Corporation. This, of course, is a measure with which the members of our party are in full accord.
This is one example of orderly planning of our economy and our economic activities. It is very much parallel to the type of thing I have been talking about in respect of this bill; that is, the need for a basic change in the direction of our economy. This is the way we must move. When representatives of the various financial institutions appeared before the committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, I found it interesting that they were unanimous in saying they do not want any controls or any further controls. Why not? From their point of view and the point of view of the profitability of their operations I can understand their saying this, but when they urge this course of action upon the

January 23, 1970
Business of the House House and the public I become suspicious. It is up to us to decide whether the people of Canada and members of Parliament are to be suckers and follow the line they advocate. I suggest the government is blind to the implication of the policies it is following and which are implied in the legislation before us. No attempt is made to exert any brakes on the growing corporate control of our economy and the growing foreign control of our economy which will affect Canada's future existence. In general, the economy of Canada cannot survive if we do not change our direction.
The economy in the world today is different from the past. A market economy approach is inadequate. The question now is who will manage and control the economy, and is there an alternative to the private corporate control. Is there to be a large measure of foreign control or will influence and control be exerted through government and a variety of other institutions? It is already pretty late in the day. The Barber commission report noted a number of implications in respect of farm implement costs and the control exercised over the farm machinery market. A relentless pressure results from advancing technology which makes it even more easy for larger corporations to obtain an even greater stranglehold on the economy. The government has the power to influence the situation if it has the guts. This bill leads members of this party to the conclusion that the government has no guts when it comes to safeguarding Canada's future welfare. The government is abdicating its responsibilities and the people of Canada will hold it to account for failing to live up to the responsibilities with which it has been entrusted.
Motion agreed, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
