Hon. Herb Gray (for ihe Minisier of
Finance) moved that Bill S-6, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act and other statutory provisions related to the subject-matter of certain of those amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to put on the records of the House an outline of the amendments to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, which are intended to be considered through this bill, with a view to providing material which can be the basis for discussions in the Finance Committee. Again, let me say the fact that I am not responding in detail to points raised by hon. members in the course of second reading of this and the preceding bills should not be interpreted in any way as implying that there are not things I have to say to deal with these particular points.
The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act governs the activities of federally incorporated Canadian insurance companies and of British insurance companies transacting business in Canada. The main part of the
January 23, 1970

act applies to Canadian companies, and most of the amendments in the bill before you relate to such companies. Where appropriate these amendments are also made applicable to British companies subject to the act.
At the end of 1968 there were 129 Canadian insurance companies subject to this act and 68 British insurance companies. In addition, the act applied to 14 fraternal benefit societies. The Canadian companies had assets amounting to about $14 billion at the end of the year, and the British companies had assets amounting to $1.4 billion in trust in Canada to cover their Canadian liabilities.
This bill deals with three principle matters, namely, a change in the system of incorporating new companies and amending existing charters, the establishment of a better and more flexible system of controlling companies that are in financial difficulty, and the expanding and broadening of existing prohibitions against investments and loans where there may be a conflict of interests.
Dealing with the first matter, it may be noted that at the present time insurance companies may be incorporated federally only by special act of Parliament, and as a consequence any change in existing charters must be made by amending the special act. It is noted that because of pressure on parliamentary time in recent years, this requirement has resulted in delays from time to time in the making of decisions with respect to applications for new charters and the amendment of existing charters.
The bill proposes the adoption of a letters patent system of incorporating companies and also a letters patent system for amending charters whether the charters are granted by letters patent or special act. The letters patent would be issued by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) under his seal and office, thereby making use of the existing machinery for this purpose. However, before this could be done, the concurrence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) would be required. This will enable the application to be investigated by the Superintendent of Insurance in the same manner as is followed now where a private bill for this purpose is presented to Parliament.
Companies so incorporated would be incorporated pursuant to the authority granted in this amendment, and would be subject to the Canadian and British insurance Companies Act. This means that although the letters patent would be issued by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs there would
Insurance Companies Act be no change in the existing position whereby insurance companies find all their governing legislation under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act rather than under the Corporations Act.
It is also proposed to establish a letters patent procedure whereby a provincially incorporated company can be continued as a federally incorporated company subject to the concurrence of the home province.
Generally letters patent will be in a standard form as described in the bill, but it is proposed to permit enough flexibility to enable the applicants for a charter to provide restrictions on voting rights and maximum limits on share ownership if they so desire.
At present, initial capital requirements for insurance companies are specified in their own acts of incorporation and thus are considered by parliament on a case by case basis. With the proposed letters patent system of incorporation it is also proposed that a minimum capital and surplus requirement be included in the act. The requirement for a new life insurance company would be $2 million, and for a new fire and casualty insurance company would be $1.5 million.
The second main amendments would establish a more extensive and more flexible system to control companies that are in financial difficulties. The present provisions permit conditions to be inserted by the minister in a certificate of registry on renewal, and also provide for withdrawal of a certificate in certain extreme circumstances. The proposed amendments would be more flexible in that they would permit the minister to impose conditions in defined circumstances without waiting for the expiration of an existing certificate. It is also proposed that the Superintendent be required to report to the minister in any case where he considers that a company is in financial difficulties or where its condition is rapidly deteriorating.
The minister, if he concurs in the Superintendent's report after giving the company a chance to be heard, would be able to take one or more of three steps. He could insert conditions in the company's certificate; he could grant the company a period of time to remedy the defect, or he could instruct the Superintendent to take control of the company's assets.
In any case where the Superintendent has control of the assets of a company the minister would be empowered to request the Attorney General to seek a court order requiring
2756	COMMONS
Insurance Companies Act the Superintendent to take control of the company for rehabilitation for winding up. In the event of control of the assets or control of a company by the Superintendent, the expenses incurred by him would be assessed against companies registered for classes of business similar to those transacted by the company in question.
In addition, the Superintendent would be empowered to take temporary control of a company's assets in any case where assets are missing or are not properly accounted for.
The third main amendment would bar investments and loans where there might be a conflict of interest on the part of those who are in a position to influence the decision of a company with respect to its investments. This amendment would prohibit investment in or loans to major shareholders in addition to existing prohibitions against loans to officers, directors, and their immediate families. Furthermore, investments in or loans to any corporation would be prohibited if an officer, director or a major shareholder has a significant interest in that other corporation.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
This amendment is sought in order to give more protection to policyholders against the possibility of investment decisions being influenced by other interests of persons in control.
Another important amendment would expand the power of life insurance companies to own subsidiaries for the purpose of enabling them to establish mutual investment funds and corporations that might carry on business ancillary to that of the insurance business. This will enable the life insurance companies to expand their services and to establish a reasonable competitive position with certain other financial institutions.
The power of life insurance companies to operate segregated funds would be somewhat expanded to increase the flexibility of this power.
Other important amendments would provide for a modified market value method for valuing securities of fire and casualty companies and would grant authority to Governor in Council to pass regulations dealing with the safekeeping of securities. Provisions would be included requiring a formal audit by auditors having similar qualifications to those under the Bank Act. This has not previously been in the legislation but in practice all companies have followed audit procedures.

DEBATES	January 23, 1970
An amendment is proposed that would require notice to the Superintendent of Insurance of the transfer of ownership of any block of stock of an insurance company in excess of 10 per cent of any transfer of stock that would effect a change in control. This requirement would not confer a veto power on the transfer but would require 30 days prior notice together with full details concerning beneficial ownership.
Mortgage loans with respect to those paid by insurance companies are now limited in any particular case to a maximum of 75 per cent of the value of the property on which the loan is made. This limit may be exceeded at present if the excess is insured through a government agency. An amendment is proposed to permit the limit to be exceeded if the excess is insured through a policy of mortgage insurance issued by an insurance company registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act or the Foreign Insurance Companies Act.
Another amendment would effect a transfer from Treasury Board to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) of certain discretionary authority and also from the Minister of Finance to the Receiver General of responsibility for the custody of securities on deposit.
Another amendment would establish an age limit of 75 years on eligibility to become a director of an insurance company. This parallels a similar amendment inserted in the Bank Act a few years ago. An amendment is proposed concerning the restriction on nonresident ownership of shares which would preserve the voting rights of a non-resident if those rights were acquired while a company was exempt from the restrictions. An amendment would change the definition of actuary for purposes of the act to require fellowship in the Canadian Institute of Actuaries. A number of other amendments are proposed to effect changes in wording and changes in a number of administrative procedures.
With respect to British companies, such of the foregoing amendments as are appropriate in the case of non-resident companies doing business in Canada would also be made applicable. In addition, there is a special amendment applicable to British companies in connection with investments of the assets of segregated funds. Segregated funds are established by some companies in connection with the issuance of variable contracts, that is, contracts that provide for a variation in benefits in accordance with the value of the assets in a segregated fund. A proposed amendment
January 23, 1970

would give British companies broader investment powers than at present with respect to the investment of assets in such segregated funds in order to put them in an equal competitive position with Canadian companies. Specifically, they would be able to invest in foreign corporate securities as well as Canadian corporate securities.
In general, the proposed amendments will improve the system of control and supervision of insurance companies for the protection of policyholders. They will also give some expansion in the powers of insurance companies to enable them to better serve their customers in their particular fields. The amendment concerning incorporation of companies and changes in charters will hopefully save parliamentary time and provide a simpler and quicker system for dealing with these matters but one which will continue to require the investigation and recommendation of the Superintendent of Insurance.
The bill also proposes amendments to three other acts. These are, in some respects, consequential upon some amendments that had been proposed to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. The first deals with the Canada Student Loans Act. It is proposed in the bill to enable insurance companies to make loans that are guaranteed by the government pursuant to the Canada Student Loans Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Amendments were introduced at the current session to the last two of these acts to enable insurance companies, trust companies and loan companies to be designated as organizations that could make such guaranteed loans. It had been proposed to effect a similar amendment to the Canada Student Loans Act through this bill. However, the House will recall that an amendment for this purpose is also contained in the bill to amend the Canada Student Loans Act which was considered before Christmas, and which is now awaiting further consideration here after the committee hearings on it. This bill covers the same area, so when the Finance committee considers it the Committee may wish to make an appropriate change to avoid overlapping.
Amendments are also proposed that would affect the powers of banks subject to the Bank Act and Quebec savings banks subject to the Quebec Savings Banks Act. At present, both chartered and Quebec savings banks may make mortgage loans, but mortgages are limited to a maximum of 75 per cent of the
Insurance Companies Act value of the real estate where the mortgages are other than the National Housing Act mortgages. An amendment is proposed in this bill that would enable chartered banks and Quebec savings banks to make mortgage loans in excess of the 75 per cent maximum where the excess is insured under a policy of mortgage insurance by a registered insurance company.
I, therefore, ask the support of this House for this Bill at this second reading stage.

subtopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation before us in the form of Bill, S-6, concerns amendments to an act governing the British Insurance Companies Act. The amendments are both technical and detailed. It is my feeling that we can hardly deal with the details of this proposal without first taking a look at them.
I note that this bill has, among its many parts, reference to insurance against accident and death and it also deals with other than life insurance. But, Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak for a few moments today on a phase of insurance which presents the greatest problem and frustration to Canadians.
Car insurance has been well described elsewhere as a service with 120 million dissatisfied customers. Indeed, this very week in the House there have been proposals from members on this side that the government should investigate the continual increase in car insurance rates. A few days ago the hon. Leader of my party, the New Democratic Party, raised a question with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford) as to what consideration was being given to intervention in the car insurance field with the idea of setting up car insurance as a federally operated business.
I should like to put a few points on record now that we have this insurance legislation before us. In my opinion, car insurance is an integral part of the over-all national picture with regard to traffic safety. I say this because we have 150,000 traffic casualties a year in Canada, including no less than 5,000 fatalities. This means 100 Canadians are slain every week. The economic toll of highway traffic injuries and repairs amounts to about $1 billion every 12 months. Of this $1 billion, car insurance costs about $600 million. That is the amount Canadians spend every 12 months to protect themselves from the war on the highways.
Regarding car insurance premiums, of every dollar spent Canadians recover only
2758	COMMONS
Insurance Companies Act about 67 cents. I think that one of the first matters which the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should investigate in the field of insurance is car insurance rates. In my mind there is no doubt at all that the importance of car insurance goes far beyond the realm of private profit and that it should, as are car licence and traffic regulations, be handled by the public for the benefit of drivers and pedestrians.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I quote briefly from a recent Canadian press story that deals with the insurance business in Saskatchewan. It says that the Saskatchewan government's insurance plan has never lost money since its inception in 1946. The plan was passed in the Saskatchewan Legislature by the CCF, predecessor of the NDP. In 1968 the surplus for that year was over $150,000. At any rate, a great surplus has been accumulated since the plan began in 1946. The present Minister of Highways in the Liberal government of Saskatchewan, Dave Boldt, is no supporter of the NDP, I am sure; but he stated recently that the insurance office pays its own taxes and grants and that private insurance firms in Saskatchewan have been asked but have never tried to submit a better plan. Before resuming my seat, I urge the government to examine all matters pertaining to car insurance rates and to see whether there is a possibility of operating the car insurance business under some sort of federally established agency.

subtopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some comments I made on an earlier bill also apply to insurance companies. I was most interested in the changes the minister outlined, and I agree that most of those changes are worth while. But he has not touched on the major problem of ensuring that moneys accumulated by Canadian citizens in the form of insurance, and held by insurance companies, shall be used for the advantage and benefit of Canadian citizens. Insurance companies hold vast sums of money which has been contributed by Canadian citizens, and unless this money is used for the benefit of, and to the advantage of, Canadians we cannot really say that insurance companies in this country are acting as agents of the Canadian people or in their best interests.
There are incorporated in this country under federal or provincial charters probably between 1,000 and 3,000 insurance companies, many of them operating in exactly the same

DEBATES	January 23, 1970
fields as other companies. I think the minister will agree when I say that there seems to be little competition in this field. Many different companies provide the same type of insurance. It seems that every time a new company is incorporated you see less rather than more competition in the insurance field. Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? Let me explain.
If there were two insurance companies in the country, both offering the same kind of insurance, you could go to Company A or Company B, and their rates would be competitive. But when you see a proliferation of companies, all involved in the same basic field, it seems that those companies join together and set rates. There is nothing the insurance buyer can do about it. Their rates appear to be exactly the same. When I go to my insurance agent and want to buy fire insurance, he opens the drawer in which he keeps the files of 50-odd companies. He appears to have some kind of unwritten agreement with those companies under which he will work through his files from front to back and, when he has reached the back of the drawer, return to the file in front. Some buyers of insurance will be interested in what happens to their insurance premiums although most will not, being only interested in buying an insurance policy. Frankly, it does not matter to me with which company the agent may place my insurance because the rates are all the same, as are the benefits.
Insurance companies in this country do not insure us against all risks. By that I mean if you want to buy insurance to cover a unique risk, you will have to go to Lloyds of London. If you plan on holding a large outdoor bar-beque and want to insure against the possibility of rain, you will have to go to Lloyds of London because no Canadian company will accept the risk. Our insurance companies may say that they are willing to provide coverage against all sorts of new risks that arise, but they do not do that.
The government also has the obligation of informing the Canadian public what insurance is really essential. It must to some extent help to change the public's attitude towards insurance. With the advent of social benefit programs, the Canada Pension Plan and other pension plans, certain types of insurance have become less and less valuable. The government must tell our people just what is the role of the insurance industry, and what the role of the private entrepreneur in this field is. I say that because in this country we seem to be working at cross purposes. Let me cite an example, Mr. Speaker.
January 23, 1970

A few years ago a man working in a northern mine died and left a widow who was either 46 or 47 years old and two children aged 13 and 14. He left her an insurance policy worth $5,000. What happened? She could not obtain mother's allowance because she had too much money; also, because she had too much in the bank she was not eligible for certain social security benefits. She was told to use up her $5,000. That is what she did; as a matter of fact, her money will run out this month. In the meantime, her kids have grown up. They are beyond the age at which she will be eligible for mother's allowance. That $5,000 did her no good. If she had not had it she would have been eligible to receive benefits under provincial and federal schemes; she would have received additional allowances for her children and, after her children were grown up, no doubt would have been eligible to receive further benefits under welfare schemes.
As things now stand, she will have to apply for municipal welfare. Clearly, that $5,000 has been subtracted from that family's standard of living. By that I mean, Mr. Speaker, that if the husband had not left this $5,000 insurance policy his wife and family would not have had to forgo forms of social assistance which would have been available to them. The wife therefore lost both ways; she lost while the husband was saving to pay the premiums on the policy, and she lost after he died because the $5,000 precluded her receiving the benefits I have mentioned. Clearly, the needs of our people in a changing society are different and I should think that any insurance agent who tries to sell endownment policies is not being quite fair.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
While there is still a great need for term and other insurance, the government, having gone into this matter, has an obligation to relate what they do in that field to the whole field of insurance. The minister is very interested in protecting shareholders. He is also interested in protecting loans and in having them secured. If you have money that you can invest in an insurance company you do not have to worry because having stock in an insurance company is the same as being able to print money.
What about the people who have to be protected? My colleague mentioned the matter of automobile insurance. Is it not time this government looked into the field of automobile insurance, at least to the extent of 21611-36*

Insurance Companies Act taking a look at third party liability automobile insurance? If two cars are involved in an accident and a pedestrian is struck, it cannot be said that the pedestrian had anything to do with the accident. He was merely a third party. The government should make it mandatory for everyone to carry this third party liability insurance. They may not be interested in protecting the vehicles involved, but innocent third parties should be protected.
In many fields we have not given any consideration to these people, but have left this up to the insurance companies. Some automobile companies have been autocratic. I wish to refer to one. When I mentioned the name of Allstate Insurance this morning I was asked if I was being fair. I wish to refer to two letters and let members judge whether I am being fair. They raise a problem not dealt with by the minister in this bill. This is the problem. If an insurance decides it does not want to pay, it says to the customer, here is your money back; you are no longer insured with us and you were not insured at the time of the accident. However, there is legislation to the effect that the company has a partial liability if it cancels a policy.

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? I am not quite sure to what the hon. member is alluding, but is it not a fact that insurance companies have to give so many days statutory notice by registered letter before cancellation?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
That is not correct, Mr. Speaker. I will read the letter because I think it explains the situation better than I can. If you have carried insurance with a company for a period of time it is true they must give you 30 days' notice of cancellation. It can be cancelled for many reasons. It can be cancelled on moral grounds.
Some hon. members will recall the famous cow case which was discussed at great length for a number of years. The government had a problem with a certain farmer. This farmer fought back in many ways, including threatening the health of the then Minister of Justice. After reading some of these reports, the insurance company decided to immediately cancel the insurance on the farmer's barn. The usual 30 days' notice was not given because the policy was being cancelled on moral grounds. The policy was eventually reinstated because the company did not have the right to do this.
The argument of the insurance company was that the farmer was going off his rocker
2760	COMMONS
Insurance Companies Act and, as a result, might burn his barn. This could have been a possibility. However, the barn could also have been struck by lightning or children could have set it on fire. The risk was no greater then than it had been the day previous. The Superintendent of Insurance eventually forced the company to reinstate the policy.

speechtext: May I be permitted to ask another question? Why was the Superintendent of Insurance permitted to do so? It seems to me the only grounds he would have for action would be the statutory conditions in the policy to which both the company and the man who held the policy subscribed at the time the policy was issued. It is a formal contract. Those statutory conditions will vary from province to province, but in the cases of which I have heard relating to automobile insurance, which is what the hon. member is talking about at this time, there is a condition that a registered letter must be sent so many days prior to cancellation. If not, I suggest any province that has been so lax in its duty should be checked up on that subject.

speechtext:
That may be true. Possibly we should get rid of the agents. I am only dealing with the problem as I know it. I do not even know the name of the company with whom I have my fire insurance. I pay a premium once every three years, and that is all I know about it.
I own an old building on the highway, a former school. It has become an eyesore. It does not have much value, but it would be expensive to tear it down. When I purchased this school from the school board I felt I should insure it because I was of the opinion that if you owned something of value it

DEBATES	January 23, 1970
should be insured. I spoke to my insurance agent about this. I suggested he decide the amount for which the building should be insured and the premium. He said he would not insure it because if it burned down, then people would say that I burned it down and there would be a lot of trouble. He advised me not to insure the building. I have had the building for ten years now and it still is not insured. Individual circumstances have a great deal to do with what happens.
I wish to quote from a letter written in 1969 to the Superintendent of Insurance in Toronto. I quote:
In August 1953 I was involved in a two car accident on Highway 11, just south of Trout Creek, Ontario. The other car was driven by a Mr. Archie Haggerty of Aitikokan, Ont., and he had as a passenger his sister-in-law, Mrs. Nellie Haggerty of Kirkland Lake, Ontario. Some time after this the plaintiffs wrote to me through their lawyer, Mr. G. Wallace of North Bay, asking for an out of court settlement of $35,000. Allstate Insurance with whom I carried a P.L. and P.D. policy for $100,000 sent a "very friendly" man around to see me and get me to sign statements. Soon after this I received a cheque from Allstate Insurance for the full amount of the premium that I had paid, with a statement to the effect that they were not covering me since I had made a false statement when I applied for the insurance.
I immediately contacted a lawyer, Mr. P. B. C. Pepper of 320 Bay St. Toronto. Mr. Pepper told me that I should have talked to him before talking to the adjuster. Mr. Pepper then told me that he would send the cheque back to Allstate and that as far as I was concerned there was no false statement. Also he said that the insurance company was bound by law to pay a basic $11,000, the amount that the Unsatisfied Judgment would otherwise have paid at that time, if I had carried no insurance.
I had bought insurance from Allstate when they first came to Canada, with Simpson Sears. There was a front page news article in the Toronto Star telling of Allstate selling insurance at large discount prices. People were lined up in Simpson's basement and the salesmen were filling out the forms as quickly as possible. When asked if I had been involved in any accidents I mentioned them, they were minor accidents. In the rush I forgot to mention a small accident for which I was not to blame, but for which we had settled 50-50 on the advice of the insurance company with whom I was insured at the time. Since the accident occurred in Sudbury it would have been more expensive to pursue the case than to fix the car.
Allstate then appointed a lawyer, Brendan O'Brien Q.C., 101 Richmond St. West, Toronto. They also had a Toronto doctor in Court in North Bay, where the action occurred in 1955, to testify that the injuries sustained by the plaintiffs would not leave any permanent disabilities. Before I took the stand in court Mr. O'Brien made a statement to the effect that I had no reason to conceal the truth in my evidence since I was fully insured with Allstate.
January 23, 1970
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Incidentally, he was Allstate's lawyer.
The judgment was for $19,400 against me. I was sure that Allstate would pay that amount. Mr. Pepper did not attend this court hearing. He told me that it would not be necessary since he was sure the lawyer for Allstate would work as hard as possible to keep the amount of judgment as low as possible.
I do not remember hearing anything more of this case until 1957. At that time the plaintiffs sought to have me examined as a judgment debtor. Mr. Pepper appeared in court and refused to have me examined on the grounds that I was insured and that the insurers had paid a sum of money into court and that the plaintiffs accepted that sum of money. I found out through my present lawyer, Mr. Dalton Dean, Q.C. of Haileybury, Ont. that the plaintiffs sued Allstate some time after the court judgment case, and according to Mr. Dean were given some $11,800 as partial payment.
The next time I heard from Mr. Pepper was by letter about the end of 1958. He said 'it is almost a year now since I last heard from the plaintiffs' and he believed in letting sleeping dogs lie. He enclosed his account at that time. Mr. Dean has that letter.
The letter continues:
I heard nothing more about the matter. Actually I had forgotten the whole thing. But last August the sheriff from the Haileybury court came here to serve me with a paper to appear at a special examiners court as a judgment debtor. I was attending a teachers' course in Toronto at the time. My wife called me there and I attempted to see Mr. Pepper.
The letter goes on to describe how he was served with papers to appear for examination and so on. It ends:
I feel I was not fully informed of all facts and was misled. I also think I should have been a party to the court action taken against Allstate, since the judgment was against me. Now Mrs. Haggarty's lawyer says that the amount of money paid into court was accepted as partial payment. But according to Mr. Pepper's letter of January 6, 1958 they accepted moneys paid into court by the insurers-no mention of partial payment.
A friend who is an insurance adjuster suggested I write to you for advice. He could not believe such a case could develop until I mentioned the word Allstate. I am enclosing some of the correspondence concerning the case.
A considerable amount of correspondence was enclosed. I raise this matter now because it is typical of three or four cases of a similar nature which are brought to my attention every year. The Superintendent of Insurance can become involved

I agree he has some say-but these cases always raised problems after an accident had occurred. After an accident has occurred, a company will often say: We cancelled your insurance on moral grounds, or because of a false statement, or because of an omission to supply certain particulars; here is your money back; you are
Insurance Companies Act no longer insured. When this happens, of course, it is difficult, if not impossible, to be insured with anyone else.
I remember that when Allstate came to Canada I applied for insurance with them. They were inviting applications, but they sent them all back with the comment: We cannot accept your application for insurance because you live in northern Ontario. They were really saying that they did not intend to insure anyone in northern Ontario. The difficulty is that having received a letter of this kind from Allstate, it becomes much more difficult to get insurance from another company. We have been supervising this insurance field as well as we can, I suppose. It is, of course, essential that every driver should be insured. It is essential that everyone who drives a car should know that the other guy has satisfactory insurance. So, insurance will have to be compulsory. It may be that the federal government should enter the field of automobile insurance at least to the extent of reinsuring motorists. It might set up some agency which would make possible the balancing out of car insurance costs across the country. This is an essential service and members of Parliament should interest themselves in this idea in order that we might devise some sensible solution to a vexing problem.
The decision has been made to impose safety standards in connection with the manufacture of automobiles and it is my hope that this principle will be applied to snowmobiles as well. Since in so many cases the requirement to be adequately insured is mandatory, I believe arrangements should be made for insurance to be provided at a reasonable price to all.
It is my opinion that the committee should take a close look at some of the difficulties which have arisen in the insurance field, bearing in mind certain of the judgments which have been handed down. No doubt the difficulties to which I have drawn attention are capable of solution. Some companies do not create these difficulties. Others do, yet all these companies are covered by the same legislation. Changes could be made to eliminate the unfairness against the individual which is sometimes shown. I hope the minister will discuss with the Superintendent of Insurance some of the steps which could be taken to make the provision of insurance much more equitable. As I say, insurance is, in most cases, mandatory. Most of us cannot dispense with it. We should therefore be able

January 23, 1970

Foreign Insurance Companies Act to carry satisfactory insurance at the lowest possible cost and with the least possibility of abuse.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the explanation given by the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) in outlining the reasons for the introduction of Bill C-134, to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. Although the wording of the bill is very brief, its application will have a considerable effect on a large number of people and at the same time will establish a new concept in international relations.
In my view this action to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act is nothing more than a government move without any principle. This is simply another piece of windowdressing, a piece of paper which is designed to confuse and delude the public into the belief that the government is doing something and is taking swift and stern action to protect the fisheries resources on both coasts. Nothing could be further from the truth.
This type of action is not new to this government. We heard the same thing away back in 1964 when the then Secretary of State for External Affairs was speaking on a bill to establish Canada's Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act. Upon the passage of that legislation the government promised the immediate establishment of geographical co-ordinates along our coasts and the drawing of base lines protecting our shores and sealing off the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Bay of Fundy as conservation areas for the development of our fishery resources.
No one could make promises in more convincing tones than the Hon. Paul Martin, then Secretary of State for External Affairs. On May 20, 1964, as reported at page 3409 of Hansard, he said:
First, the bill establishes the fishing zones of Canada at 12 miles from the coast line. When it is passed by parliament and proclaimed, Canada will have a fishing zone in the 3 to 12 mile area off our coast line. This, in the view of the government, is a fundamental achievement of the bill. It is not enabling legislation in this respect. On proclamation, the 12 mile fishing zone will be established. I must emphasize there is no doubt, and there can be no doubt, about this point.
There may not have been any doubt in the minister's mind when he made that statement, and now that he is resting comfortably in the other place we know that all his doubts
January 23, 1970	COMMONS
and fears have vanished and he could not care less about our depleted fishery resources. But I would point out to you, sir, that we are now in the year 1970 and the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Bay of Fundy on the east coast, and Dixon entrance and Queen Charlotte Sound on the west coast are not yet closed to foreign fishing fleets.
In all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, is it any wonder that our fishermen look with mistrust and suspicion at any proposals put forward for their benefit by this Liberal administration? The record of broken promises, hopes raised and destroyed, fishing resources depleted as a result of Liberal procrastination is there for everyone to see. The record of the Liberal administration since 1963 in relation to our fishermen and their problems is abominable.
What did the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) say as recently as November 2 when speaking in the Throne Speech debate? He warned this House, as recorded at page 414 of Hansard, that the North Atlantic fisheries resources of Canada are in grave danger of "overfishing" by foreign fishing fleets. He said:
The total fishing effort, the international fishing effort in the North Atlantic, has more than doubled over the past decade.
He also told us that just beyond the 12-mile limit off the west coast of Vancouver Island he saw during the past summer a Russian fleet of 40 giant trawlers, every one of which was bigger than a British Columbia ferry. The minister painted a graphic wordpicture of the danger that the east and west coast fisheries resources might soon be completely destroyed by foreign fishing fleets.
This is a serious economic problem covering vast sections of our nation on both the east and west coasts; it is a problem which affects the livelihood of large numbers of our people, who by reason of their location and education are unable to move or qualify for any employment other than fishing. Faced with this serious situation, what does the government plan to do? It proposes to enact Bill C-134.
Let us look carefully at this proposal. Under the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act as it now stands, no foreign fishing vessel may enter Canadian fisheries waters unless authorized to do so by regulation under the act, by any other law of Canada, or by treaty. No person from a foreign fishing vessel may buy supplies in Canada unless similarly authorized.
DEBATES	2767
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
In essence, the act has two methods of protecting Canadian fishing grounds. The first, or chief method is by preventing foreign fishing vessels from entering Canadian fishing grounds, or, alternatively, permitting them to enter but making them subject to Canadian fisheries laws or otherwise restricting their methods of operation. The second method is incidental to the main method, which is forbidding the foreign fishing vessels from coming into Canadian ports for the purpose of selling their catch or buying provisions or water.
In my view, the proposed amendment is an insipid and questionable attempt to strengthen the means of control. No one will deny that it is highly desirable to have the fishing operations of foreign fleets curtailed on both coasts. But there is a right way and a wrong way to do it, and in my opinion the method proposed will do nothing to alleviate the present situation and may well, in fact, compound the problem.
The government apparently interprets the wording of the act as meaning that a supply ship of a foreign fishing fleet is not and cannot be classed as a fishing vessel, and therefore it has the right, under maritime law, to come into a Canadian port and take on supplies for a foreign fishing fleet that is despoiling Canadian fishing grounds, without the necessity of getting a permit or being subject to being refused a permit.
The government now asks this House to amend the meaning of "fishing vessel" as defined in the act to include a supply ship of a foreign fishing fleet. By this action the government hopes to prevent or control the complete destruction of our fisheries resources by refusing to provision supply ships of foreign fishing vessels, or perhaps get them to agree to observe our conservation laws in return for provisioning them.
This measure can only be classified as a childish solution of what is in effect a mansized problem. The proposed legislation reminds me of the actions of a disgruntled little boy who takes his bat and ball and walks out of the ball game when he does not get his own way. This type of action never has worked, and it will not work now because the ball game will still go on.
In my opinion, the government is using this amendment as an excuse for its inaction in establishing over-all base lines around our coast and as an excuse for its inaction in dealing with international fishing problems
2768	COMMONS DEBATES	January 23, 1970
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act which have a considerable bearing on the well-being of Canadian fishermen.
I believe the present wording of the act which defines "fishing vessel" is sufficiently wide to class a supply ship of a fishing fleet as also a fishing vessel. After all, the present definition is not exclusive or exhaustive. It says that a fishing vessel "includes"-not "is" or "means"-"any ship or boat or other description of vessel used in or equipped for fishing or processing or transporting fish or marine plants."
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Surely, a supply ship of a fishing fleet is a vessel that is necessary and incidental to a number of fishing vessels, and can therefore be classed as a fishing vessel. After all, a supply vessel has merely more water-tanks and more storerooms than an ordinary fishing vessel.
The corresponding conclusion that could be drawn from the government's interpretation is that fishing vessels that are watered and provisioned by a supply ship are not really fishing vessels because they do not carry adequate water and provision facilities with which to complete their voyage. What nonsense, Mr. Speaker!
On its face, the amendment would mean that the present restriction as to the granting or the refusing of permits will apply to all supply and auxiliary vessels sailing with foreign fishing vessels off Canada's east and west coasts. But, Mr. Speaker, there has been a long tradition in east coast ports of supplying visiting fleets. Trade with these fleets is estimated to run as high as $10 million or $12 million in St. John's Newfoundland, and some $3 million in Halifax and Sydney, Nova Scotia.
This tradition is based on two facts. One historic fact is that the North Atlantic fisheries were fished for at least three centuries before confederation, by fishing vessels sailing out of Europe, and during this period eight nations have established recognized fishing rights in the North Atlantic fisheries. In fact, these eight nations are granted greater fishing rights than Canadian fishermen on our own shores. The fishermen of Spain, Portugal, Italy, France, Norway, Denmark, the United Kingdom and the United States have the right to fish up to three miles from our coastline, while Canadian fishermen must pursue their fishing operations 12 miles from shore.
This was one of the promises made by the former Secretary of State for External

Affairs speaking on May 20,	1964, on
Canada's Territorial S'ea and Fishing Zones Act, when he said that the fishing operations of the eight countries I have mentioned would be phased out. More than half a decade has passed since this promise was made. The Liberal government stands today indicted and condemned by our fishermen for its inaction on their problems, because fleets from these eight countries have still not been phased out and they still operate up to three miles from our coast. Yet on November 3 last the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) stood in his place in this House and said that those who are familiar with fisheries laws-I am paraphrasing his words-now know that we in Canada have an exclusive 12-mile limit. Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister, exclusive to whom? Certainly it is not exclusive to Canadians. It may be exclusive to the eight fishing nations I have mentioned- exclusive to the fleets of France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, the United Kingdom, the United States, Norway and Denmark, but it is not exclusive to Canadians. Let that be put on the record now, and let us hear no more of this double-talk until the government takes action on this really important problem.
Second, Mr. Speaker, if Canada refuses to provision the fleets which are destroying our fishery resources we will not achieve our objective because alternative sources are awaiting the opportunity to supply them. At the present time the common market countries are building a huge supply base on the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, and even without this gunboat policy the fleets of other countries will soon be getting the major portion of their supplies from St. Pierre.
This amendment, therefore, should not be applied to our east coast ports as a prohibition against the provisioning of foreign supply ships or fishing vessels, because it will only anger the countries concerned without limiting their fishing activity on our shores.
It is my understanding that on the west coast there are no such fishing traditions. However, if we refuse to supply the Russian and Japanese fleets with water, I do not believe we will seriously cripple their operations because they can readily turn to American ports to the south such as Seattle, Everett, Olympia and Bellingham. In fact, the Russian fleet must pass Bellingham in order to get to Vancouver. Alternatively, the Russian fleet could get water and supplies to the north of us at Ketchikan, Juneau in the American Panhandle, or at Petersburg and
January 23, 1970

Wrangell. Therefore, a prohibition on the supply of water, as stated in this amendment, for application to the west coast would have little meaning. According to my information, Russian ships take on only fresh water in Vancouver, but no provisions or fuel, and since fresh water is available elsewhere this amendment is pointless and futile.
As with the east coast situation, the west coast problem-toward which the minister said this amendment is administratively directed-will not be cured by small-boy scare tactics. Even more than the east coast, the west coast fisheries are in imminent danger. Unlike the east coast, the continental shelf on the west coast extends seaward only 11 to 46 miles, if the information is correct which was given to the Fisheries Committee when it met in that area. The fishing grounds, therefore, are tremendously concentrated and extremely susceptible to overfishing and destruction. Already there are fishing fleets there from Japan, Russia and South Korea, and there is no reason why they will not be joined soon by fleets from the Philippines and other nations of southeast Asia.
In my view, the tactic of striking at the supply ship is itself an admission that Canada agrees to the presence of these foreign fleets, that Canada intends to take no rational action to protect the fishing grounds off its shores but simply intends to harass these fleets-and by harassment anger the nations which send them.
This amendment is useless as a solution to the preservation of our fisheries resources. I say this because it attacks only the incidental problem, which actually is not a problem at all if the main problem is solved. In my opinion, this amendment will only annoy those nations that fish our resources on the east and west coasts and will in the final analysis prevent a proper approach to the problem. This approach must, and can only be made at the negotiating table. It must be made by Canadians talking common sense to their opposite numbers.
The common sense approach would be to point out to all concerned, at an international conference on the conservation of our fishing resources, that there are only so many fish on the fishing grounds of the North Atlantic and the west coast. These resources can be ruined for years or completely destroyed by overfishing or by the use of destructive fishing gear. It must be pointed out that these resources can be preserved for ourselves and for future generations only if we agree to

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act conserve them in our time-and our time is now. In my opinion, it is mandatory that this action be taken through international negotiation and agreement.
I cannot help but wonder why this bill has been brought in by the Minister of Fisheries. Here we have a problem which concerns many of our European allies in NATO, some of our European trading partners and the great fleets of Russia and Japan; but instead of getting our External Affairs Department to cope with it, we see the Fisheries Department trying to implement a childish, gunboat policy which it is incapable of enforcing on the nations concerned.
We cannot help but wonder what is happening in our External Affairs Department. Have we no friends left in the world? Have we sacrificed all our integrity on the altar of recognition of Red China, to the exclusion of all our former friends and allies? I am beginning to wonder who stands up for Canada. And when the going gets tough and rough at some future date, I wonder who will stand by us.
Could it be, since we have backtracked on our word to the free Chinese on Taiwan, that no one trusts us any longer, that we are looked upon as fickle and inconsistent in the role we play in international affairs? Surely the amendment before us will not reduce the strength of the fishing fleets on our east and west coasts by one ship or one lifeboat. It certainly will not win us any friends at any future international bargaining table where ultimately the problem of our diminishing fishing resources will have to be discussed. What frightens me, Mr. Speaker, is that on its record the government seems incapable of talking common sense to other nations, and to some nations it cannot talk at all. It has scored debating points, but it has never arrived at agreements.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In my opinion, Bill C-134 may win the battle of the supply ship but it will cost us international agreement on measures to preserve our fisheries resources. Having stated our concern over this measure, it is not our intention to move any amendments at this time because there may be a movement for a particular province to take advantage of the bill in its present form. We therefore look forward, Mr. Speaker, to a more detailed explanation of the specific impact of this bill in certain areas when it comes before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry for study.

Mr. Speaker, I did not rise on the point of order, but I appreciate the effort of the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) to bring some sort of order into our proceedings this afternoon. I rise in light of the fact that we have before us in Bill C-134 a proposed amendment to the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. I wish this act included the protection of our coastal fisheries from the

Liberal government, and in particular the Liberal House leader.
I was somewhat annoyed earlier today when the government House leader lightly dismissed the idea of dealing with fisheries matters by suggesting that we pass three bills next Wednesday afternoon. I shall not enter into the procedural hassle we had earlier, except to say it is very awkward when one is preparing, in good faith and on the strength of the word of the government House leader, to deal with a certain bill only to find that we have passed one other bill and that the next order of business is another bill entirely.
I once rather annoyed a former Minister of Fisheries by stating in the House that the government tended to treat the Department of Fisheries as the Cinderella of government departments. The events that have taken place today seem to indicate that this is the disposition of the present Liberal administration. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I suppose I should proceed to make some comments on the substance of the amending bill that is before us.
In his few remarks the minister indicated that he did not consider this to be a bill which would end all the problems faced by our seacoast fisheries. I concur in his sentiments in this respect. This bill may be a step in the right direction, but I think it warrants further examination in committee because it is a little difficult to understand how it will act as a lever in regard to negotiations on operations of foreign fishing fleets off our coast.
I appreciate full well that the situation in regard to the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act and the operation of foreign fishing fleets off our coasts is not identical on the west coast and on the Atlantic coast of Canada. The approach that one takes in respect of the need for this amendment may, therefore, be slightly different depending on the point of view of the member who represents a coastal constituency.
The question that immediately comes to my mind is that of the operation of a large fleet of Soviet vessels offshore on the west coast and, in this last season, offshore of my own constituency at Vancouver Island. I think I can see some relationship between what is proposed in this bill and the operation of that fleet, although I am not sure that I understand how this measure will provide any protection from it.
If the minister makes any remarks in closing the debate on second reading, he should

clarify this matter; if not, it should be clarified in committee as it relates to certain remarks of the member who preceded me and referred to Russian vessels calling at American ports to take on water.
My impression has always been that they were not permitted to do that, and that this amendment would have the effect of precluding Soviet supply vessels coming into Canadian ports to take on water or other supplies to assist in the maintenance of their offshore fleet. The minister is as aware as I of the mood of the fishermen of the west coast at the present tune and in particular of the west coast trollers. Some of them may have remarked to him, as they have to me, that if they find Soviet vessels in their way in the future, as they have in the past, they will take potshots at the pilot-houses. If one relates this bill to the question which I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) a couple of days ago in regard to the plans of the government to provide protection against fleets such as the Soviet fleet of trawlers and, in particular, the government's views on a proposal placed on the Order Paper by a British Columbia member-that is, Bill C-91-one realizes that the bill is only calculated to deal in a very minor way with the problem faced by the fishermen of the west coast as a result of the activities of foreign fishing fleets.

speechtext:
that Bill C-175, to establish the Canadian Saltfish Corporation and regulate interprovincial and export trade in salt-

fish, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I move second reading of this bill, secure in the knowledge that it will receive support from all corners of the House. I know there will be a few minor amendments proposed in committee. Some of them may be necessary to improve the act, but basically this is a sound piece of legislation-one which will be universally welcomed, particularly in the Atlantic provinces.
We have needed a Saltfish Corporation for more than a century. I am sure of this, because it has been recommended by numerous royal commissions and special committees set up over the years to look into the problems and prospects of the saltfish industry.
The saltfish industry, as everyone knows, was the first industry in Canada. It was the first industry on our shores and certainly the first industry the white man knew in North America. In some ways it is still an antiquated industry. Certainly it can stand a good deal of improvement.
The bill to establish the Canadian Saltfish Corporation in effect puts the credit of all the people of Canada behind the saltfish industry, which is now mainly concentrated in Newfoundland, along the north shore of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, Quebec, and on the coast of Labrador. At one time it encompassed all the Atlantic region of Canada and much of the New England coast as well. It contracted in size as the fresh fish and frozen fish industries developed. It is now limited in great measure to small, remote communities along Canada's east coast.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is served by inshore fishermen, with limited means and small boats, who often do not go out beyond the sight of land. These people live in modest circumstances. They are enterprising, God-fearing, hardworking people prepared to take great risks, including risking their lives. One hundred thousand of these people have very limited opportunities in their own local areas. They live in communities which range in size from a few houses to several hundred. There are approximately 1,000 communities in this category which depend almost exclusively on the production of saltfish, primarily the catching and manufacturing of salt cod which can be shipped anywhere in the world and will retain its quality for months, even in the hottest climate. This industry is being carried
January 23, 1970

on in small, remote communities and around those communities there is little opportunity for other gainful employment.
One thing that impressed me very much is that the opportunity for employment in the forest industry, particularly in Newfoundland, is more limited today than it was ten years ago. Approximately half as many people work in the forests of Newfoundland as worked there in the mid-fifties. More men are in fact engaged in the inshore salt fish industry in Newfoundland because there are half as many jobs in the woods. This situation calls for dramatic action by the federal government to help these fishermen gain not only a larger share of world markets but a better price for their product.
I am convinced we can add considerably to the income of these fishermen merely by bringing into being a fish development marketing organization. But we will do more than market fish. Through rationalization I am sure we will be able to improve the facilities available to these fishermen in order that they may improve their product, upgrade it for the markets of the world, tailor the qualities and grades to market requirements in order to improve their sales prospects and in turn improve their income. This is the main objective of the development corporation.
The corporation will be a single-desk selling agency selling on a worldwide basis. It will be selling in the Caribbean and Mediterranean countries principally. It will be selling in a market for saltfish which has been surprisingly stable for several decades its volume has remained almost constant. What has gone wrong from our point of view is that Canada has been left with a smaller and smaller share of that relatively constant world market. If we put the accent on quality, meeting market requirements and upgrading the product so that it is more acceptable to foreign buyers we will be able to considerably improve this fishery.
We have a parallel piece of legislation. Members are familiar with the establishment of the Freshwater Fish Market Corporation last year. This corporation will operate in much the same way. In May of this year I hope to announce the schedule of prices for saltfish so that fishermen will know at the beginning of the season what their product is worth. They will be paid as they deliver their fish, rather than having to wait until the end of the year to receive any income whatsoever. They will know what they are going to

Canadian Saltfish Corporation receive in terms of income and will be able to plan with some confidence for the future.
At the end of the year the corporation will take whatever surplus it obtains as a result of this selling exercise, and pay it out to the fishermen in proportion to their catch and sales. This corporation will be the sole buyer of saltfish throughout the Atlantic region. It will have that power because all the provincial governments have indicated that they are interested in our national legislation. They will provide the necessary provincial power to make the corporation function effectively.
I think most hon. members opposite and many on this side of the House are familiar with the problems of the saltfish industry and the inshore fishermen. I can think of no single factor that can contribute more to his income and feeling of accomplishment than the passing of this bill which, at long last, will make the saltfish industry the fisherman's industry as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the minister's statement concerning an act to establish the Canadian Saltfish Corporation and regulate interprovincial and export trade in saltfish. I have a few comments to make on this legislation.
The marketing of saltfish and the regulating of interprovincial and export trade in this commodity is a problem that has for many years been troubling the industry in Atlantic Canada. We on this side therefore approve in principle the government's bill and will do everything within reason to expedite its progress through committee. However, there are some questions concerning the method of operation of the corporation which we would like answered. Hopefully, our doubts in this direction will be satisfied by the minister and his officials when they appear before the committee; if not, we have amendments which we are prepared to put forward in order to strengthen and improve the bill.
For almost 500 years fishermen of many countries have reaped the codfish harvest of our North Atlantic fisheries. In return, the North Atlantic has exacted its price in the lives of those fishermen, in the loneliness and widowhood of their wives and in the orphaning of their children. The history of the people of the Maritime provinces, Newfoundland and Quebec, is interwoven with the history of the fishing industry.

Canadian Saltfish Corporation codfish on the shores of these provinces are part and parcel of Canada's constitution and inheritance. In fact, the trade of these provinces in salt cod with the West Indies, South America, Spain, France, Portugal and Greece has established ties of friendship and trade with these countries which are older than Canada.
For some years past the salt cod industry has been relatively unimportant in terms of gross national product because the fishermen who live by that industry have, despite their efforts, been unable to earn sufficient income to make a contribution to income tax revenues.
It would appear that the salt cod industry is a special craft industry of individuals and families which should now be collectivized and organized in the hope that this action will bring about its continued survival. I sincerely hope this bill represents the answer to the Canadian saltfisherman's problems. However, in my opinion this collectivization or organization should not be so ruthless or so intent upon efficiency that it forgets to take into consideration the human factors involved.
The dislocation of the lives of these fishermen and their families where it occurs

and it will occur-must be softened by a spirit of compromise and adjustment on the part of the government as well as by the compromise and adjustment that will be demanded of the fishermen. With this thought in mind, I believe that the chairman and president, as well as the directors of the corporation and the members of the advisory committee should in the best interests of this corporation be from those provinces which participate in the administration of the act, a fact which is not spelled out too clearly in this bill.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
As I understand it, the purpose of this bill is to bring greater economic benefits to the primary saltfish producers in Atlantic Canada. This is a worthy objective, and in light of the low annual income recorded for this area it is a very necessary and worth while project. In fact, attempts to make the saltfish industry profitable have for many years occupied the attention of five provincial governments and the federal government.
Whatever remedies have been brought forward and tried, the salt-cure fishermen have, prior to this legislation, lacked a regional corporation with power to control the interprovincial and export trade in saltfish, a corpora-

tion with capital sufficient to acquire modern methods of assembling, curing, grading, processing, packaging, storing, selling and engaging in market promotion. The phasing-out of traditional but inefficient methods of curing, a reduction of duplication in costs which should bring increased returns to the fishermen, are ends which I hope will be realized under the proper management of the corporation proposed by this legislation.
The minister said the objective of the corporation at the outset is to increase the income and improve the living standards of producers. We hope that in pursuing this objective-and it is a proper one-the corporation will not lose sight of the fishermen of Labrador, of the Quebec Gulf and North Shore, of Prince Edward Island and of Nova Scotia who also are in vital need of assistance.
It is a regrettable but necessary provision of this bill that fishermen who fail to meet the terms and conditions imposed by the board will not be able to sell to the corporation. In effect, they will not be able to sell in the interprovincial or export markets. This will result in the unemployment of those unfitted by experience for any other employment. Processing plants which are dependent on the catches of these men will go out of business. However, it would appear this is the price which must be paid if the saltfish industry is to survive and if a proportion of the fishermen are to enjoy a reasonable standard of living.
In view of these facts, the corporation should not operate, in my opinion, strictly within the narrow confines of this bill. I believe the corporation has wider responsibilities. Once it is established it should alert, as early as possible, the various agencies of government, both federal and provincial, to these foreseeable disruptions. I say this in order that employment facilities, retaining facilities, pension and welfare facilities and financial aid by way of government loans to small businesses, be made known to unemployed fishermen, the employees of redundant fishing plants and to the small businessmen who operate these plants.
As I stated earlier, the five provincial governments of Atlantic Canada have in the past given much thought to the problems faced by the saltfish industry. In fact, on October 29, 1964, the Atlantic Salt Fish Commission, headed by Mr. Finn, tabled its report outlining a summary of its conclusions and recommendations after consultation with the pro-
January 23, 1970	COMMONS
ducers and processors in Atlantic Canada. This is a very interesting report, full of salty phrases and saltfish problems, and the commission's final conclusion was that the saltfish industry was not then ready for a saltfish marketing board.
According to the commission's report, the basic difficulty was the low productivity per unit of the fishermen involved. If that conclusion of the commission holds true today, the marketing corporation proposed in this bill may, in fact, do a good deal of damage. Indeed, the damage done might well offset the amount of aid provided unless the corporation proceeds with compassion, acting in close consultation with the rehabilitation and social agencies of the federal and provincial governments in the Maritimes, Newfoundland and Quebec. I say this knowing that the provinces I have mentioned already have the highest unemployment rates in Canada and the lowest standard of living. We must always be mindful of this situation and careful to do nothing by way of legislative action which would compound then- problems.
These fishermen need help, and hopefully the corporation to be set up under the bill before us can give it to them. However, the problems which this new corporation will face are likely to differ entirely from those faced by the management of the Fresh Fish Marketing Corporation. I would remind hon. members that the latter corporation has a virtual monopoly of fresh fish and can therefore control its quality, its rate of delivery and its price in our major market, the United States.
This is not the situation which will face the saltfish corporation. When it is set up, this corporation will be in a position to control the export trade in saltfish as it relates to production in Canada, but when it comes to selling saltfish abroad it will not benefit from a monopoly because it will have to compete in world markets with other great saltfish-pro-ducing nations such as Iceland, Norway, Spain, Portugal and Denmark.
This presents a challenge to our Atlantic coast fishermen inasmuch as the success or failure of the corporation to be set up by this bill will depend in great measure upon the quality of the saltfish products which it can offer in world markets. This means the corporation must be headed by men who are knowledgeable with regard to the saltfish industry and its markets, men who are willing to work in closer co-operation with the

As I stated earlier, some salt codfish fishermen in Atlantic Canada may become unemployed as a result of the board's consolidation of effort. Although it may succeed in providing continuous employment and a higher standard of living to some, the board must always be conscious that it will have failed in its over-all objective if its operations raise over-all unemployment figures still higher, lowering further the present low standard of living.
In his speech of November 3, 1969, on fisheries matters, the Minister of Fisheries said many things with which I agree. He also expressed many anomalous views with which I disagree, though I shall not now debate them with the hon. gentleman. For example, he omitted to mention the tremendous buildup of the Canadian fishing fleet, with the resultant prosperity of our shipbuilding and processing plants brought about by the constructive programs initiated during the Conservative administration under my right hon. friend for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
The minister went on to mention the plans for the fishermen proposed by his own government and, as reported at page 411 of Hansard, he listed the various bills to be considered. He then stated that the government also proposed to change the Unemployment Insurance Act, commenting that the question of unemployment insurance was of great interest to our fishermen.
This, of course, was the understatement of the year. Unemployment insurance is a subject of great interest to the entire industry, including the processors. There is nothing in this bill to indicate the stand which the government plans to take with regard to this important matter. As the minister is aware, fishermen are now classed as being selfemployed, as sharing in a joint venture. Will this classification still apply to fishermen landing fish for the Canadian Saltfish Corporation? If not, what changes is the government planning along the lines referred to in the minister's speech? The answer to this question would be very helpful. I hope the government gives an early indication of the changes it proposes to bring about in this important field.

Mr. Speaker, in his opening remarks the minister said that "at long last" this bill would bring to an end the system which meant that the salt codfish producers of Newfoundland were prisoners of the merchants and the storekeepers. It was a timely phrase and it brought to my mind my visit to the province of Newfoundland in 1955, at which time many people were telling me that they would like to see legislation of this kind brought about.
I may say that I found myself to be a member of what was then the marine and fisheries committee of this House, shortly after my first arrival here. As a result of that, and because I had personal knowledge only of the fisheries of the Pacific coast, I embarked upon a trip to Newfoundland one fall and spent four weeks in that province. It was one of the most delightful and interesting experiences of my life.
I spent most of that time visiting the people in the small fishing villages, or outports of what was then considered to be quite a new province of Canada. I was regarded very largely as a curiosity from the mainland. The fact that I was a Canadian made me somewhat different in the eyes of many people.

I was going to refer to a publication which was issued by our Department of Fisheries and Forestry quite recently, Fisheries Reports No. 11, in which one of the footnotes points out that in a report made in
