1964 a detailed study established the income of the fishermen at less than $1,000 per year, inclusive of transfer payments, which makes the interjected figure of $800 somewhere close to the mark.
I mention this to underline that when the minister said that this piece of legislation is being brought in "at long last," there is certainly no quarrel from this part of the House that the economic situation of most fishermen in Newfoundland leaves much to be desired. I noted that the minister emphasized this situation in his remarks on this bill, and for that reason there is perhaps relatively little controversy in the House in dealing with it.
If I understand it correctly, the genesis of this bill stems from the Federal-Provincial Fisheries Conference which was held in Ottawa in January of 1964. Certain events have flowed from that conference. The minister mentioned one of them, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Board, and suggested quite rightly that in some ways this is a companion piece of legislation dealing with another of Canada's fisheries.
I made some reference back to the presentations which were made to that conference in 1964 by the government of Newfoundland, in which they indicated that they were proposing something along the lines of the bill that we have before us. At page 32 of the presentation to the conference by the government of Newfoundland, dated January 20, 1964, the following statement appears:
The programs necessary for the strengthening of the Newfoundland fishing industry can be divided under three general headings:
1.	Marketing and price stabilization.
2.	Inspection and quality control.
3.	Rationalization and development measures.
The marketing of saltflsh in Newfoundland has a long history. If I recall correctly the picture which was painted to me at the time I was in that province, it indicated that while there was a form of co-ordinated fish marketing at that time, the real control still rested in the hands of what were often referred to as the great merchants of St. John's. One of the things about which we require assurances- an assurance which is not found in the bill- is that the enactment of this legislation will in fact represent a transfer of power from those financial interests in St. John's, which have traditionally controlled the fisheries and kept the fishermen at a subsistence level, to the fishermen themselves.
The idea of a marketing board is one that all of us in this House can easily support. The
January 23, 1970

brief of the province of Newfoundland refers back to the days when the Canadian Wheat Board was established, as the first piece of legislation providing for the orderly marketing of a product. But one of the things this bill does not clarify is whether in fact the fishery of Newfoundland will be under public control and under the control of the producers, or whether it will be left in the hands of what in the terms of the wheat farmers would be called the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. This question is not clarified in the bill.
This board is set up as a Crown Corporation. The officers and the directors are to be appointed by the Governor in Council with one appointee from each of the participating provinces. There is to be an advisory council which says that two thirds of the members shall be connected with saltfish production. But whether in fact this legislation will at long last bring about a transfer of control into the hands of the producers of Newfoundland depends entirely upon the approach which the government takes to the administration, the approach which the government takes to the appointment of the people who are going to form the board of directors of this corporation.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In committee we will require an explanation as to the emphasis to be placed on having the Crown corporation become an agency for the processing of fresh fish, and the emphasis to be placed on maintaining the existing structures for the processing of fish. I recognize there is a complex pattern throughout the industry and that the existing machinery for marketing cannot be done away with overnight. However, I think this is the kind of assurance those of us in this party want. We want assurances that in fact the operation of this measure will be such as to ensure to the fishermen the maximum return possible for their product.
We know that, even at best, the return to the fishermen for saltfish will not be anything magnificent, given the present situation with respect to world markets and the price levels that prevail. Those of us in this part of the House insist that this should be made clear as far as the people in the Atlantic fisheries are concerned.
I was glad to hear the minister say, if I heard him correctly, that all the provinces involved in the production of saltfish have indicated their desire to participate in this

Canadian Saltfish Corporation program. I was glad to note that one of the things to be achieved is the solution of a problem of concern to many people in Newfoundland, and I presume indirectly to fishermen in some of the other provinces; that is, this body will operate as an interprovincial corporation and will bring to an end the unceasing warfare that existed in previous days regarding the marketing of fish through the authority of one province or another. This was a matter of concern to the fishermen of Newfoundland when the province entered confederation. It was a matter of concern in respect of the marketing of Newfoundland fish products during the early years Newfoundland operated within confederation.
This bill meets, in part, a concerted desire of the people of Newfoundland in particular, as expressed to the former leader of the Liberal party, as far as it parallels the kind of marketing board that has been developed for the marketing of Canadian farm products, particularly those from the three Prairie provinces. If the Minister of Fisheries has not already taken note of this, I should like to refer him to a letter which the Premier of Newfoundland wrote to the former Prime Minister on February 13, 1963, when he was Leader of the Opposition.
Parts of this letter were quoted not once but twice during the proceedings of the conference in 1964. The concluding sentence of the statement made to Mr. Smallwood by Mr. Pearson when he was speaking as Leader of the Opposition is that we should have the following:
-a federal-provincial program for fishery development to be founded on the principle that national action for fisheries should parallel the action already being taken, and action to be taken, for agriculture.
Perhaps this bill is in part a fulfilment of that pledge. I am not suggesting it is the complete fulfilment. I mention this to the minister because he admits himself it has been a long time coming. I made a special trip to Ottawa before the opening of the session of Parliament in 1964, full of hope and optimism that out of that Federal-Provincial Fisheries Conference we would have introduced during that session of Parliament interprovincial marketing legislation. I suppose it is always better to have something late than never. In this respect I find myself echoing the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he comments on matters relating to pensions. It seems that it takes a long time for ideas to penetrate the heads of members of the Liberal government.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT-REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, in so far as many of us are concerned, is a milestone in the history of the ancient saltfish industry. I have waited for this legislation for a long time, like many other people in Newfoundland.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
At long last we see in this bill what we hope will be the fulfilment of the expectations of the Newfoundland fishermen who have waited 20 years to see the fulfilment of the promise of Confederation with Canada. I could not help feeling a little disappointment

today as I listened to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) when he spoke on second reading of this bill. I was disappointed the minister made light of the subject and missed the opportunity he had to sum up the historical factors leading up to and indeed directly influencing the legislation now before us.
I am also disappointed that the bill is before us at a time when members are getting ready to leave for the weekend and when it is obvious we have only a few hours at our disposal. If we had the time which this legislation warrants, I or others who may be able to do it much more adequately would be able to tell this House the heartbreaking story of Canada's most ancient industry, the saltfish industry. However, the minister did not choose to have this debate on another occasion. I am sure his motives were good. As a matter of fact, I feel he did not expect to have to deal with this legislation today.
The minister knows better than I do the importance of getting this legislation on its way. Until this bill receives royal assent he knows the industry, which is suffering the disastrous consequences of last year, is in a state of suspended animation. The longer the delay in the passage of this legislation which received first reading on December 19, the greater the opportunity, for those who are critical of the bill, to tear it down. Justice delayed is justice denied.
So we are prepared to get this bill on its way and before the committee. I may be forgiven, however, if I make a few brief observations. Other remarks I would have made at this time I shall save for the committee stage, the report stage or third reading of the bill. Before I do so I would make a suggestion to the minister. He may not think it is really relevant.
With the passage of this legislation and the setting up of this corporation, carrying with it as it does the final recognition of the importance of the role in our economy of the inshore fishery, we hope there will be the ancillary result of making the iniquitous and unjust centralization program redundant. This is a cruel, unjust and inhuman program of moving the people of Newfoundland from their ancient homes to centralized ghettos which will have as its only effect the facilitation of the administration of welfare.
We hope the passage of this legislation will carry with it a recognition of the importance of the industry in spite of what Mr. Finn in his report and others have said through the years about the inshore fishery having no
January 23, 1970

future and there being no future in saltfishing. As a result of this bill we hope that cruel program of centralization of which we have heard so much and about which the Canadian people have heard some disturbing reports will no longer be necessary. I say this notwithstanding the fact that the administration of the program has now passed from the minister of fisheries to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. We hope this bill will spell the end of that program.
There are in the bill a number of things which concern us. The minister referred to them as being minor amendments. We consider them to be major amendments. We consider, for example, the provision in the bill whereby the corporation will be empowered to make loans to fishermen to be a major item and one which in fact does not go far enough. If this bill in fact destroys the feudal system under which the saltfish industry is conducted in Newfoundland, it must by definite legislative steps eliminate the economically crippling credit system which is now the hallmark of the saltfish industry and which deprives the fisherman in many instances of a fair return for his labour.
We consider this to be a major item and hope the minister will heed the suggestions we will make in the committee in respect of the provision of a special fund which would be self-revolving to ensure that, regardless of whether the fishermen had a good or bad year, they would not have to suffer the consequences of the manipulation of interest rates and the imposition of a stricter credit regulation by the corporation. This corporation cannot, and indeed must not, function as an ordinary commercial corporation.
I make no apology, and I am sure no one from the province of Newfoundland would make any apology for saying that. We hope there will also be provision for the setting up of a fund of at least $1 million. I have not pulled this figure out of the hat. It is a figure suggested to me by those who should know what they are talking about. I believe $1 million or $2 million should be provided for this revolving fund to ensure that the fishermen at the beginning of each season have guaranteed, adequate funds with which to outfit themselves, and that there will be proper regulation and a fair and just rate of interest.
Only in this way can we ensure that there is and end to the feudal system whereby the fishermen in return for being outfitted in>
the spring of the year are obligated to give their entire catch to the merchant without knowing

Canadian Saltfish Corporation how much they might expect in return. This is what is known as the iniquitous open-receipt system of buying fish. We consider this a major item. Even though we consider this a good bill, and even though we commend the minister for introducing it and think he is a good minister, we are also sure he is anything but infallible.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We could have preferred if he had taken some of us into his confidence so that we could have given him our constructive suggestions in a more informal way, rather than having to make them in debate in this House or through the formal technique of amendments in committee.
We would also like to see an expression of intent spelled out in the bill, if for no other reason than to ensure that the corporation does not conduct itself as a purely commercial corporation. The philosophy of the bill should be spelled out in the preamble. It was quite adequately spelled out by the minister in a statement which he made at St. John's, and I quote his words:
Immediate objectives of the proposed corporation are to improve and stabilize the earnings of primary producers of cured cod fish. This would be achieved by maximizing returns from the trade and minimizing costs in assembling, processing and' marketing operations.
We would like to see that in the preamble of the bill. The minister may not occupy his portfolio in two years' time, and we should take steps now to make sure that those who follow know what was the intent of Parliament when this bill was passed.
The bill provides for the appointment of' five directors. The appointments will be made by the Governor in Council, which in this case means the Minister of Fisheries. It could conceivably happen that the five directors could come from Bay Street, or the equivalent street in Vancouver. The president could come from the west coast and the chairman of the board from Montreal. Unless they knew what Parliament had in mind when it passed the bill, they could forget that its primary purpose is to maximize returns to the primary producer, the fisherman.
I would not want the impression to be created abroad that this bill is merely establishing a marketing board. If it is to fulfil our expectations, it must be much more than that. This is not to suggest that marketing is not one of the principal functions of the. corporation.
2780	COMMONS DEBATES	January 23, 1970
Canadian Saltfish Corporation
Because of the ancient system of marketing in the trade, we have been losing our main markets to competitive countries such as Iceland, Denmark, Norway, Portugal and Spain. Exporters have failed to recognize the changes that are taking place in our principal markets for cured fish. Those markets are now more sophisticated than ever. Here I speak of our principal markets in Jamaica, Barbados, Trinidad and Puerto Rico. Salt codfish, which is their principal source of protein, is now sold in local supermarkets with the aid of attractive packaging. Our exporters have failed to compete in this manner. They have failed to take account of the fact that in many of our principal markets salt codfish is a political football. A marketing board will be in a better position to deal with governments than individual exporters.
We feel that the corporation must have a presence in our export markets; it must have representatives in those markets. Indeed, it may have to build cold-storage facilities close to those markets in order to ensure that the product is adequately safeguarded. Notwithstanding the minister's opening statement, it is a perishable product and on occasion has suffered the consequences of being left on wharves in the West Indies for long periods of time. For this reason it will be necessary for the corporation to enter into agreements with the governments of Jamaica and other West Indian countries to build cold-storage warehouses in which the product can be stored.
We must do a better job in our principal markets by the adoption of new marketing techniques, new packaging and the elimination of the middleman. In many cases these principal markets have become fragmented, to the detriment of the saltfish fishermen.
The corporation will also have to determine in advance market requirements so that fishermen in future will not produce and cure fish on a hit-and-miss basis. At the beginning of a season the corporation will have to determine the grade of fish the Jamaican market will require. Then, as the sole purchaser of fish, it will be able to go to the fishermen and say, "We will require so many quintals of such a cure of fish for this market." The fishermen will know exactly what they have to produce, and they will produce it. This will bring some order into the chaotic situation that now exists in the industry. Without exception, improvements can be made in every one of our markets. They have to be made if we are to eliminate the archaic thinking that has caused so much damage to the industry.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I note that the bill calls for the setting up of the corporation's head office in St. John's, Newfoundland. I suggest that this is the obvious place for the corporation to have its headquarters because St. John's will be the principal centre of its operations.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I also suggest that the president of this corporation be a resident of the area in which the corporation is located, and somebody who has an active knowledge of the industry. Above all, Mr. Speaker, it should not be a political appointment. I leave that suggestion with the minister.
We look forward to studying this bill in committee. Many people have made representations to us and in committee we will be passing many of them on to the government. We hope the committee will get together very soon and deal with this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues on this side of the House, I welcome this legislation. I commend the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) for the initiative he has shown in tackling it and, we hope, putting an end to the old feudal system that has for centuries been the curse of the fishing industry of Newfoundland.
Those of us from Atlantic Canada, and especially from Newfoundland, have been looking forward with great anticipation to the legislation which we are now debating. We realize how important this legislation is to the fishing industry in Newfoundland and, indeed, to the other Maritime provinces. We also appreciate the minister's willingness to pay attention to the suggestions and arguments we have advanced in favour of this board and the corporation as outlined in the bill.
The minister is well aware of the representations made to him and the government, and the consistency of our efforts to impress upon them the absolute need for greater government involvement in the saltfish industry of Atlantic Canada. He is also aware of the pressing need for an organized effort by the government to regulate the processing and marketing of our salted cod.
One does not need to be a prophet or to possess divine inspiration to predict what will happen to the saltfish industry of eastern Canada without this type of legislation, without active participation by the government in the processing and marketing of the product.
January 23, 1970

It is regrettable that it has taken so long to have this board established. As my colleague from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) said a few moments ago, Newfoundland has been waiting for this opportunity since confederation, and we have lost 20 years. Let us hope that the board will function to the advantage of the people for whom it is intended, that is, the producer-the fisherman himself.
The average fisherman has been too long the victim of the old feudal system. The history of the fishing industry in my province has been one of exploitation, hardship, and in too many cases near-starvation for those engaged in it. For too long were we content to accept what always appeared to be inevitable as far as our fishermen were concerned, that is, they must learn to roll with the punches, take it on the chin and be satisfied to accept a standard of living far below the national average and one that would not be tolerated by people in any other part of this nation. A moment ago I said that our fishermen had been exploited for centuries. Of course, the reason is obvious-the system under which they have been compelled to operate lends itself to abuse and exploitation.
Can you imagine, sir, the people engaged in the fishing industry selling their catches on an open-receipt basis? Can you imagine any person today, engaged in any other industry in Canada, working all summer and not knowing what he will earn? But that situation has existed in Newfoundland for decades and, possibly, for centuries. Men fished all summer; they shipped or took their fish to the exporter and were given an open-receipt without knowing how much they would get. They took potluck, and come fall they hoped to obtain enough money to square their bills with the merchants and have a few dollars to spare.
If one were to compare the life of the average Canadian with that of the Newfoundland fishermen, it would be very interesting. The fisherman of Newfoundland has an average annual income of $900 or thereabouts. For that he must work during the fishing season from before daylight until after dark. He must constantly face the hazards of the seas, and is forced to run risks when battling the elements that would terrify t he average Canadian. He must conquer his fears and overcome the fury of the Atlantic. Total dependence on his own ingenuity and resourcefulness has instilled in him a fierce sense of pride and independence. The average fisherman is by nature a rugged individualist 21611-37

Canadian Saltfish Corporation who works hard for his living. He would much rather battle the elements than accept social welfare.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation will have the effect of improving the lot of the average fisherman of Atlantic Canada, and especially of Newfoundland. I am therefore delighted that it has been brought in. We have suggestions to make in committee which we hope will improve the bill.
There is one thing I must say, because it has a bearing on the success of the fisheries in my riding and in most other parts of Newfoundland. I hope that the government will go a step farther and not merely stop with the establishment of the Saltfish Corporation. I believe it will be necessary for the government to make sure that adequate facilities are provided whereby fishermen can land and process their fish under sanitary and proper conditions. If the fishermen are to take full advantage of this legislation, adequate facilities must be provided for them.
If our fishermen are to comply with regulations pertaining to quality and sanitation set out in the bill, facilities must be provided. Those facilities should include landing and processing facilities, community wharves and the like. When the bill comes before the committee I hope the minister will indicate that my suggestions will be incorporated in the government's program, which is designed to encourage the saltfish industry. We must make sure that our fishermen derive the fullest benefit from the proposed corporation.
I also think the minister should look at the herring fishery, especially in Newfoundland. People who are eminently qualified to speak on the subject have suggested to me that we should consider prohibiting the use of large herring seiners in our bays. I have been informed that am unlimited world market exists for this very high-protein food. I am told that 95 per cent of the herring caught are used for oil rather than human consumption. I think this industry would perform a much greater service to humanity if greater emphasis were put on the nutritional and protein value of herring as food for human consumption, rather than reducing an estimated 95 per cent of the catch to oil.

I hope the minister will give thought to providing facilities which the fishermen want, and that consideration will be given to a certain group of people in Newfoundland. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add my comments on Bill C-175 to establish the Canadian Saltfish Corporation, not only because, as most of my colleagues have said, it is a good bill but because I feel it may be the answer to many of the problems which exist in the fishing industry in my district. I commend the Minister Of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) for the positive approach he has taken since taking over the fisheries portfolio, and for the legislation he has already put forth since taking office. However, as is the case with most legislation, there are bound to arise many unforeseen human errors. I am sure the minister would agree that this is true with regards to some of the past programs which were instituted on behalf of the fishermen.
The bill to establish the Canadian Saltfish Corporation is a good one but I, along with others, have some reservations and I would like to point out some weaknesses, not to criticize for the sake of criticism but in order to offer positive suggestions which have arisen out of my assessment of the weaknesses in most of the past legislation and programs which were designed to cure the ills of the fishermen. There are peculiar problems in various parts of the Atlantic region, which necessitate a special appoach.
If I may make a general over-all criticism arising out of my short experience of politics, in assessing the fishing industry I believe it is a weakness in correlating and providing a system or plan whereby all the various programs support one another. If I may offer an example, I supported wholeheartedly the deficiency payment program. That was a good program but it seriously missed the boat in my district due to certain unforeseen factors.
21611-37^
Canadian Saltfish Corporation The deficiency payment program was an interim measure intended to compensate for the extraordinary situation which depressed the fishermen's income in 1968, and to avoid its recurrence in 1969. Payments will be made after February 1 on various grades of fish classified as to quality and character, such as light-salted, heavy-salted and split fish. I spent two weeks during the summer visiting many of the fishing villages in my riding, and in not one case where I inspected fish could I find any distinction made as to grade. Fish was purchased as one grade whether it was prime, maderia medium or small. Naturally, the fishermen lost out because they were paid according to the whims of the buyer. So again fishermen suffered because there was no grading or culling of fish. When they get the 50 per cent difference between the 1968 price and the target price, they will lose out on the greater difference which would exist if they had sold their fish by grade.
This emphasizes the fact that you can have all the programs you want, however good they appear on paper and however sincerely they are prepared-and I assure the minister that he has all my commendation for his sincerity-but what was the good of the deficiency payment program to the fishermen of the northwest coast of Newfoundland, when they were deprived of their livelihood because of the weak restrictions on fishing limits by the foreign draggers who appeared for many months in last year's fishing season?
As admirable as the deficiency payment program was, what is the point of deficiency payments when there are no fish to be caught? What good are deficiency payments if there is no culling and the fishermen are not given the advantage of trying to produce a better product, which the experts say should be done? We can have all the individual programs we want, and we can produce them on paper until they fill all the offices on Parliament hill, including the House of Commons, but we will never succeed unless we support the programs not only with money but by factors involved. This takes into account the fishing grounds, the facilities required and, most important of all, the guidance and leadership which we have not given the fishermen up to now. Equally important, we must have confidence in the fishermen who have the practical knowledge necessary and need our help.
Let me speak about some of the better-programs which have been introduced! through the initiative and good intentions of
January 23, 1970

Canadian Saltfish Corporation the government. Let us look first at the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, whereby an individual fisherman or a group of fishermen can get loans up to $25,000 at a preferred rate of interest in order to buy a boat or to purchase fishing gear or equipment. They have ten years to pay it back.
This is a good program because it gives the fisherman-on paper, mind you-the opportunity to get a loan at a bank or other lending institution, which he might not get under normal banking regulations, because it is guaranteed by the government. This program is designed to give fishermen with resourcefulness and initiative an opportunity to get themselves started in a competitive way in the fishing business. This is truly a wonderfully program, on paper. Just try to get a fisheries improvement loan in the province of Newfoundland! Just ask the many hundreds of fishermen in my district of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe about this!
During my two years in politics I have found that only two fishermen in the whole province were granted loans under this program, and in order to find those two I had to take the word of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), after reading the list produced by his department. The staff of the office of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) is aware of the number of times I have asked for material on fisheries improvement loans to send to my constituents because of my faith in the program. Of the many hundreds I have sent out, only one man indicated he was able to get a loan from the bank in his area. He got the loan, but not through the plan under which he applied as laid down in the act. He was granted a loan which he could have obtained anywhere, and was charged 11.9 per cent interest instead of having the advantage of the preferred rate under the act. This is why I say we must have some confidence in the fishermen who are supposed to be encouraged. As far as Newfoundland is concerned, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act is not worth the paper on which it is written.
Unless these matters are investigated and leadership is given to support the fishermen, we will never give them a decent start. Perhaps the loans offered under this legislation will overcome the serious lack of trust in those for whom its benefits are intended. I certainly hope that is the case.
The resettlement program is also good on paper but leaves much to be desired when put into practice. This emphasizes a lack of proper appreciation of its intention. The main

weakness here is the lack of infrastructural logistics in providing the public facilities required in growth centres, in order to properly receive those who are relocated. We can designate growth centres for as long as we want, but they must be capable of providing the necessary facilities to allow a new resident to get the new start in life which the program is designed to give him. Again there is a lack of intersupport for the program.
I could give members many examples of frustration in this regard, but the one that sticks in my mind refers to a man who came to see me about welfare. He started out in one community with two motor boats, a horse, a truck, 23 sheep and his own garden in which he produced all the needs of his family. He enjoyed life.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
After making three moves, he ended up a stone's throw from the community from which he started and is receiving $112 a month in welfare for himself and a family of five. Without dwelling on all the other good programs, provincial and federal, such as the Fisheries Act, the Coastal Fisheries Protection regulations, the fishing vessel indemnity regulations and the fisheries loan boards, I suggest there must be an interrelationship with other departments of federal jurisdiction such as Public Works and Regional Economic Expansion.
I become a little tired and frustrated when I receive the same stock answer to requests for breakwaters, community-stages and other facilities which the fishermen must have in order to derive any benefit from this new corporation. In answer to the many requests I make of the Department of Public Works, I receive a similar tale of woe. I am told that on investigation it was found that due to the fact that the number of fishermen is decreasing over the years, and that the fisherman's income is decreasing, it is found uneconomical to accede to my requests.
I ask the minister how he expects the number of fishermen to increase, or their income to increase, if in the first place they do not have the necessary facilities. Let me refer to one example in the community of Anchor Point. I quote from a letter received from the provincial member of the district, who is also the provincial Minister of Public Works:
With reference to Anchor Point, this, as you know is one of the most prosperous settlements in St. Barbe North with some of the best fishermen on the whole northwest coast-
January 23, 1970

I have been endeavouring for the past few years to get a breakwater and combination community stage and freezer, as well as a haul-up and Ash drying area... I do hope you will do your utmost to try and secure these requirements during your term of office.
Well, I have tried. I am sure the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), as well as the district directors, know that I have tried for the past 18 months. I receive fine answers of agreement but then I hear the familiar tale of woe. I am told that departmental investigations reveal that about 52 fishermen operate 44 boats and use the public wharf facility. They say they agree there is a need, but unfortunately funds are not available; or that it is the view of the department that a community-stage, a fresh fish holding unit or a bait-holding facility are not required. I ask when they will be required. Are we waiting for the fishermen to become so discouraged that they go on welfare?
I hope to have an opportunity to deal with my misgivings about the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and its responsibilities in relation to the fishing industry in Newfoundland. But in the desire to complete the debate today I shall leave this question until I have another opportunity. I hope the authority vested in the Saltfish Corporation will be a means of overcoming the problems regarding loans. I hope the attitude of the banks in denying fishermen with initiative and resourcefulness an opportunity to obtain a loan to improve their lot as fishermen will not be adopted by the corporation. If I might be so bold, I would suggest that the criteria used for granting these loans must not be on the basis of the fisherman's security, because he has not been given the opportunity to build up any security due to the failure of past legislation to protect him and his industry.
I should like to make one final comment in respect of liaison and communication. There has been a complete lack of communication, by officials below the level of district officer, with the fishermen. I hope when the advisory boards and advisory committees are appointed we will realize the extreme importance of consultation with individuals or groups in all areas. This must be done even if it is necessary to enlarge the committees. I hope there will be no skimping in respect of staff, and that the officials will go to the fishing communities to explain the benefits under the act
Canadian Saltfish Corporation and to give the guidance and leadership required in order to produce a better quality of fish and so improve the income of the fisherman. There is also great need for communication with the many development associations which have sprung up and are becoming involved in the problems of their communities and districts. They are there to help, and I hope we will listen to the grassroots advice they offer for the good of all concerned.
I hope that every section of the province will be represented on the advisory committees, because of the peculiar problems that exist in their communities. Let us forget political appointments and screen-out the capable and the devoted rather than the patronized.
I join others on this side of the House in support of this bill, Mr. Speaker. I hope the minister will take the suggestions in the spirit in which they are intended, to produce the best legislation possible and to build a base out of the resources that have been staring us in the face for hundreds of years. Let us by co-operation and good will gain the respect and the confidence of the fisherman in the Atlantic region by showing him that he is deserving of equal opportunity with all other Canadians.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT-REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill is of great interest to the fishermen of the Gaspe district and of the Quebec North Shore. As it is nearly six o'clock, I will be very brief as I would like the bill to be referred to the committee as soon as possible. Besides, I will have an opportunity to discuss the matter when third reading of the bill is moved.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT-REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my appreciation to hon. members for their patience and courtesy in working overtime this afternoon, listening mainly to members from Newfoundland talking about fish. But it is Friday anyway, so it is appropriate.
I do not oppose the principle of Bill C-175, an act to establish a Saltfish Corporation and saltfish. I, along with my colleagues from Newfoundland, welcome it and we congratulate the Minister. We congratulate him for at least trying, which is more than many of his predecessors appeared to do.
2786	COMMONS
Canadian Saltfish Corporation
This measure is being hailed in some quarters as the end of all the problems for the fishermen engaged in the saltfish industry, or to use the $5 word, the panacea for all their problems. I am afraid I do not share in this enthusiasm. I wish it were so, but it is just not so.
As a Newfoundland fisherman would say, the minister has "a noggin to scrape," meaning a very difficult task, if this new corporation is to be instituted and truly used to improve the lot of the fisherman. We have seen many plans and schemes come and go which were ostensibly intended to aid the fishermen but ended up as the means whereby those other than fishermen could afford winter holidays down south, palatial homes and Cadillac comfort. I hope that this is truly the start of a real breakthrough for our Atlantic fishermen engaged in the saltfish industry. For the new corporation to be successful I think we must constantly remember its duties expressed in clause 23(b) as "increasing returns to fishermen." I think this is the line that should stand out. All members of the corporation should be aware of it at all times.
I am concerned that in the bill I see quite a large part devoted to inspection and policing of its provisions, including quality control, but no provision is spelled out whereby assistance and advice are given to our hundreds of small producers of saltfish, to help them produce a product as efficiently and as sanitarily as possible, ensuring that it will pass a rigid inspection and consequently result in the highest possible return to the fishermen. It is not enough to have an army of inspectors turning thumbs down. The reasons for such rejections must be pointed out, steps taken and assistance and advice given to correct them.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I do not think a grant limited to $100,000 to be spread over the five participating provinces, for the initial establishment of the corporation, is very generous at all. Surely, this corporation for which almost everyone expresses such great hope and enthusiasm, could have a little better send-off than this. Surely, the minister's colleagues who hold the purse-strings could be convinced to share a little more in the minister's enthusiasm.
For centuries, Mr. Speaker, the marketing of saltcod produced in Newfoundland has been done by sloppy, slipshod, hit-and-miss methods. I am delighted that a serious attempt is to be made in the area of con-
[Mr. Peddled
DEBATES	January 23, 1970
trolled marketing including packaging, etc., with regulations by the corporation governing all export and interprovincial trade in saltfish. Rigid quality control coupled with aggressive, imaginative marketing could raise the lowly saltcod to the prominence which such a delicious, nutritious and valuable food deserves.
Mr. Speaker, apart from our export trade in saltfish, it never fails to amaze me that so many people right here in Canada have never heard of Newfoundland saltcod. They do not know what they are missing. I blame the government of Canada and the government of Newfoundland for not promoting this delicacy and introducing it to our fellow Canadians across the country, as well as the export trade.
I remember last year, while the Standing Committee on Transportation was visiting St. John's, Newfoundland, the committee members were invited to the home of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) to enjoy the hospitality for which the Jamiesons are famous. There was a magnificent spread, Mr. Speaker, turkey, ham, hot dishes, cold dishes and God only knows what else. The Kelligrew's soiree had nothing on it. But the dish which really appealed to the members who were representative of all Canada was the traditional Newfoundland fish and brewis. I took particular note of the way the 20 or 30 mainlanders savoured this delicacy. It may be that their appetites were a little whetted by the stimulant known as screech, but the fact remains that they did go back for second and third helpings. While the Jamiesons may have had ham and turkey next day, I doubt if they had "fish and brewis".
I hope that one of the first things the corporation does, along with promoting export trade, is aggressively promote the sale of saltcod in our own country and the rest of North America. If the name must be changed from saltcod to some fancy-sounding name, and if it must be dressed up in a candy-striped package to appeal to our discerning and advertising mesmerized fellow Canadians and fellow North Americans, then let's do it. We in Newfoundland are a captive market, Mr. Speaker-half a million souls who produce nothing that I know of that our fellow Canadians consume. From the time we turn down our Quebec-made bedcovers in the morning, step out of our Quebec-made pyjamas, use our Ontario-produced toothpaste in a bathroom equipped from Ontario, and through the livelong day, everything that we
January 23, 1970

put on, rub on or spray on comes from another part of Canada.
We are a captive market and I feel there should be some reciprocal trade. In that way, Mr. Speaker, not only would we be getting the goodwill of the Canadian people with regard to our produce, but I think we would be showing our export markets that indeed we have a good product-it is fit to eat because we eat it ourselves. I do not blame the people of Canada but, as I said before, I blame the government for not long ago adopting an aggressive and imaginative program for putting this product on the local market. There may then be such a demand from world markets that we would be surprised. Canadians are very well respected, and I am sure our saltfish would be too.
Of course, I also hope that demand for salt-fish will be strong and that we may be able to keep up with that demand. I am very serious about this and would like to see local markets promoted and see the product enjoy some respect.
1 know the minister must be given some time in order to close the debate, so I will say no more. May I indicate, however, that I shall have some questions when we come to the clause by clause consideration of the bill in committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT-REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not say very much in this debate, other than applaude the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) and his constituents. I could make many observations and talk longer on this subject than other members of the House, because in my constituency more people will be affected by this legislation than those in any other constituency. I think I can say that without fear of contradiction.
We are happy with this legislation. Even though all hon. members will not benefit to the same extent as I and my constituents, I am glad to see they are supporting the legislation, the credit for which must go to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) and not the Premier of Newfoundland. I shall have more to say about that in committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT-REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first thank all hon. members here who have contributed in the debate, and, more particularly, those who have resisted speaking at some length this afternoon with a view to making a solid contribution in committee later. As hon. members know, the best work is done in commit-

Canadian Saltfish Corporation tees. I am glad to be able to get the saltfish legislation before our committee next week.
I wish to say very few words. We are talking about approximately 20,000 fishermen and, if you include their dependents, 100,000 people, all of them resident in the Atlantic region. By and large they are on the bottom rung of the income ladder in this country and yet they are among the hardest working people in Canada. Obviously we owe it to them to provide the best legislation we can. As some hon. members have said, this is only a beginning and, as others have said, we must integrate this legislation with other legislation which exists now and which is to be brought along. I agree with both comments.
The main objective of this particular piece of legislation must be the improvement of the incomes and the lot of those engaged in the saltfishery. Some remarks earlier may have left the impression that some of the people who produce saltfish in the Atlantic region will not be able to sell their product. That is not true. This corporation must buy all saltfish offered in the areas which come under the act. In other words, all saltfish offered for sale will be bought.
Of course, the corporation must have some discretion as to quality and it will increasingly put emphasis on high quality and pay top prices for that quality and reduce the price for the poorer qualities. To repeat, anyone offering saltfish will be able to find a market for his product. The area within which the corporation must buy the saltfish offered will include, I believe, all the territory within the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, all of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, I understand that only the north shore along the Gulf of St. Lawrence will be included in the legislation passed by the province of Quebec, but not the Gaspe. One of the reasons I believe is that saltfishing in the Gaspe is relatively prosperous. It has concentrated on very high quality; the Gaspe cure is famous and the area's product sells principally in the United States. This shows, of course, why the saltfish corporation should stress quality and what it may do in future in promoting saltfish in the markets of the world and promoting a product of which we will be proud.
There was reference to a crown-owned corporation backing out private enterprise. My impression of the industry really is that we need all the enterprise that we can get, not only the enterprise of the fishermen but also
January 23, 1970

Canadian Saltfish Corporation all the enterprise of the existing trades. There is no problem here except perhaps in southern Nova Scotia. The Nova Scotia government has agreed with us that several qualities of saltfish, for the time being, will not be included under the act, those being principally the boneless saltfish produced in southern Nova Scotia principally for markets around New York.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It is possible under the act to exclude any grade or quality of saltfish. A province may exclude particular areas, if they wish, from the ambit of this corporation. It is my expectation that in Nova Scotia the boneless product will not be included under the act. It will be brought in by a change in regulations, but the province would have to concur in this. I think one of the worries of the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) is removed in that connection.
I think I can end where I began. The fisherman has been looking forward to some action
along these lines from government at both the provincial and federal levels. This corporation, if well managed, will give him a price for his product which he deserves and which he will earn. We must have other related programs in the Department of Fisheries and in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I believe the Saltfish Corporation is a good start. It is a sound idea. It is a corporation in which I have confidence and which I believe will be well run. I look forward to hearing constructive suggestions in committee next week.
